// @ts-nocheck
import "jsr:@supabase/functions-js/edge-runtime.d.ts";
import { createClient } from "https://esm.sh/@supabase/supabase-js@2.39.3";

const corsHeaders = {
  "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*",
  "Access-Control-Allow-Headers": "authorization, x-client-info, apikey, content-type",
};

function json(body: unknown, status = 200): Response {
  return new Response(JSON.stringify(body), {
    headers: { ...corsHeaders, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    status,
  });
}

// Roles allowed to administer accounts. Source of truth = the DB row for the
// caller's auth.uid(), never JWT metadata (user_metadata is user-editable).
// 'owner' is included because the owner console (owner/Users.tsx,
// owner/Businesses.tsx) provisions owner accounts and a new business's first
// super-admin through this function. The owner's own "DigiCom Business" is
// NULL (unscoped), so the create-time tenant-force below no-ops for it and the
// owner supplies the target business explicitly; super-admin/admin callers are
// pinned to their own business.
const ADMIN_ROLES = ["super admin", "business owner", "admin", "owner"];

// Business owner is protected: only the platform owner may create, edit,
// delete, or suspend a business-owner account. The DB trigger can't see the
// real caller through these service-role writes, so this function enforces it.
const BIZ_OWNER_PROTECTED_MSG = "Le propriétaire de l'entreprise ne peut être modifié que par la plateforme.";

// Map raw Postgres / GoTrue errors to messages a human can act on.
// supabase-js AuthApiError can surface an opaque body whose .message is "{}"
// with no usable .code, so regex-parsing alone is unreliable — the caller passes
// a `context` so we can give an actionable message even when the error is opaque.
function friendlyError(err: any, context?: "email" | "password" | "create"): Error {
  let serialized = "";
  try { serialized = JSON.stringify(err); } catch { /* ignore */ }

  // Safe shape log (no PII values) to aid ops debugging.
  try {
    console.error("manage-users error shape:", JSON.stringify({
      context,
      status: err?.status ?? err?.statusCode,
      code: err?.code,
      name: err?.name,
      msgType: typeof err?.message,
      msgLen: typeof err?.message === "string" ? err.message.length : null,
      keys: err && typeof err === "object" ? Object.keys(err) : null,
    }));
  } catch { /* ignore */ }

  const hay = [
    err?.message, err?.code, err?.error_description, err?.msg,
    err?.details, err?.hint, err?.name, serialized,
  ].filter((p) => p !== undefined && p !== null && p !== "")
   .map(String).join(" | ").toLowerCase();

  if (/users_username/.test(hay)) {
    return new Error("That username is already taken in this business. Choose a different one.");
  }
  if (/users_email_key|email_exists|already.*registered|registered.*another|email.*already.*(use|exist)|duplicate.*email/.test(hay)) {
    return new Error("That email is already used by another account on the platform. Emails are unique platform-wide.");
  }
  if (/email_address_invalid|invalid.*email|email.*invalid|invalid format/.test(hay)) {
    return new Error("That email address is not valid.");
  }
  if (/weak.*password|password.*at least|password should be|password.*short|password.*requirement/.test(hay)) {
    return new Error("Password doesn't meet the requirements: at least 6 characters, including an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, and a number.");
  }
  if (/duplicate key/.test(hay)) {
    return new Error("A unique field (email or username) is already in use.");
  }

  // Context-aware fallback when the provider returns an opaque error.
  if (context === "email" || context === "create") {
    return new Error("That email can't be used — it's already registered to another account or is not a valid address.");
  }
  if (context === "password") {
    return new Error("Password doesn't meet the requirements: at least 6 characters, including an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, and a number.");
  }
  const raw = (typeof err?.message === "string" && err.message.trim() && err.message.trim() !== "{}")
    ? err.message.trim() : "";
  return new Error(raw || "Operation failed. Please review the fields and try again.");
}

// ── WhatsApp instance assignment helper ────────────────────────────────────
// access shape: { mode: 'none'|'all'|'specific', instance_ids?: string[], business_id?: string }
async function applyWhatsappAccess(supabase: any, userId: string, access: any) {
  if (!access || !access.mode) return;
  // Wipe existing assignments first — this function is the source of truth
  await supabase.from("whatsapp_user_instances").delete().eq("user_id", userId);

  if (access.mode === "none") return;

  const businessId = access.business_id;
  if (!businessId) {
    throw new Error("whatsapp_access.business_id is required when mode is not 'none'");
  }

  if (access.mode === "all") {
    await supabase.from("whatsapp_user_instances").insert({
      user_id: userId,
      business_id: businessId,
      instance_id: null,
      scope: "all",
    });
    return;
  }

  if (access.mode === "specific") {
    const ids: string[] = Array.isArray(access.instance_ids) ? access.instance_ids : [];
    if (ids.length === 0) return;
    const rows = ids.map((iid) => ({
      user_id: userId,
      business_id: businessId,
      instance_id: iid,
      scope: "explicit",
    }));
    const { error } = await supabase.from("whatsapp_user_instances").insert(rows);
    if (error) throw error;
  }
}

// ── Mediabuyer Google Analytics property scoping ────────────────────
// access shape: { mode: 'none'|'all'|'specific', ids?: string[], business_id?: string }
async function applyGaAccess(supabase: any, userId: string, access: any) {
  if (!access || !access.mode) return;
  await supabase.from("mediabuyer_ga_access").delete().eq("user_id", userId);
  if (access.mode === "none") return;
  const businessId = access.business_id;
  if (!businessId) return;
  if (access.mode === "all") {
    await supabase.from("mediabuyer_ga_access")
      .insert({ user_id: userId, business_id: businessId, ga_connection_id: null, scope: "all" });
    return;
  }
  if (access.mode === "specific") {
    const ids: string[] = Array.isArray(access.ids) ? access.ids.filter(Boolean) : [];
    if (ids.length === 0) return;
    const { data: valid } = await supabase.from("google_analytics_connections")
      .select("id").eq("DigiCom Business", businessId).in("id", ids);
    const allowed = (valid ?? []).map((r: any) => r.id);
    if (allowed.length === 0) return;
    await supabase.from("mediabuyer_ga_access").insert(
      allowed.map((id: string) => ({ user_id: userId, business_id: businessId, ga_connection_id: id, scope: "explicit" })));
  }
}

// ── Mediabuyer Meta ad-account scoping ──────────────────────────────
async function applyMetaAccess(supabase: any, userId: string, access: any) {
  if (!access || !access.mode) return;
  await supabase.from("mediabuyer_meta_access").delete().eq("user_id", userId);
  if (access.mode === "none") return;
  const businessId = access.business_id;
  if (!businessId) return;
  if (access.mode === "all") {
    await supabase.from("mediabuyer_meta_access")
      .insert({ user_id: userId, business_id: businessId, meta_connection_id: null, scope: "all" });
    return;
  }
  if (access.mode === "specific") {
    const ids: string[] = Array.isArray(access.ids) ? access.ids.filter(Boolean) : [];
    if (ids.length === 0) return;
    const { data: valid } = await supabase.from("meta_ads_connections")
      .select("id").eq("DigiCom Business", businessId).in("id", ids);
    const allowed = (valid ?? []).map((r: any) => r.id);
    if (allowed.length === 0) return;
    await supabase.from("mediabuyer_meta_access").insert(
      allowed.map((id: string) => ({ user_id: userId, business_id: businessId, meta_connection_id: id, scope: "explicit" })));
  }
}

Deno.serve(async (req) => {
  if (req.method === "OPTIONS") {
    return new Response("ok", { headers: corsHeaders });
  }

  try {
    const supabaseClient = createClient(
      Deno.env.get("SUPABASE_URL") ?? "",
      Deno.env.get("SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY") ?? "",
      {
        auth: {
          autoRefreshToken: false,
          persistSession: false,
        },
      },
    );

    // ── Caller authorization (complete mediation) ─────────────────────────
    // The router now requires a valid JWT to reach this function, but any
    // authenticated user of any role would pass that gate. Because this
    // function runs on the service_role key (above RLS/column policies), it
    // must authorize the caller itself: resolve the bearer to a user, then
    // require an admin role from the DB (not from JWT metadata).
    const jwt = (req.headers.get("Authorization") ?? "").replace(/^Bearer\s+/i, "");
    if (!jwt) return json({ error: "unauthorized" }, 401);
    const caller = createClient(
      Deno.env.get("SUPABASE_URL") ?? "",
      Deno.env.get("SUPABASE_ANON_KEY") ?? "",
      { global: { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${jwt}` } }, auth: { persistSession: false } },
    );
    // getUser(jwt) — explicit token. The no-arg form needs a client session, which
    // this stateless service client never has, so it 401'd every call.
    const { data: { user: callerUser }, error: callerErr } = await caller.auth.getUser(jwt);
    if (callerErr || !callerUser) return json({ error: "unauthorized" }, 401);
    const { data: me } = await supabaseClient
      .from("users")
      .select('role, "DigiCom Business", backup_root')
      .eq("id", callerUser.id)
      .maybeSingle();
    if (!me || !ADMIN_ROLES.includes(me.role)) return json({ error: "forbidden" }, 403);

    const { action, userData, userId } = await req.json();

    if (action === "create") {
      // backup_admin is grantable ONLY by the backup_root account; backup_root is
      // never settable through the app. Destructuring strips both from `rest` so
      // they can't ride in via the service-role writes below.
      const { email, password, name, username, role, whatsapp_access, ga_access, meta_access, backup_admin, backup_root: _backupRootIgnored, ...rest } = userData;
      if (role === "business owner" && me.role !== "owner") {
        return json({ error: BIZ_OWNER_PROTECTED_MSG }, 403);
      }
      if (me.backup_root === true && typeof backup_admin === "boolean") {
        rest.backup_admin = backup_admin;
      }
      // Tenant scoping: a created account always belongs to the caller's own
      // business, regardless of any "DigiCom Business" the client supplied.
      // (Owner rows are the exception — enforce_owner_unscoped() nulls it.)
      if (me["DigiCom Business"]) rest["DigiCom Business"] = me["DigiCom Business"];

      const { data: authData, error: authError } = await supabaseClient.auth.admin.createUser({
        email,
        password,
        email_confirm: true,
        user_metadata: { name, username, role },
      });

      if (authError) throw friendlyError(authError, "create");

      const { data: profileData, error: profileError } = await supabaseClient
        .from("users")
        .insert([{
          id: authData.user.id,
          email,
          name,
          username,
          role,
          ...rest,
        }])
        .select()
        .single();

      if (profileError) {
        // Compensate: roll back the auth user so we don't leave an orphan that
        // blocks future creates with the same email.
        const { error: delErr } = await supabaseClient.auth.admin.deleteUser(authData.user.id);
        if (delErr) {
          console.error("create rollback failed — orphan auth user:", authData.user.id, delErr);
        }
        throw friendlyError(profileError);
      }

      // Apply WhatsApp instance assignments (sellers only — caller decides)
      try {
        await applyWhatsappAccess(supabaseClient, authData.user.id, whatsapp_access);
      } catch (waErr) {
        console.error("applyWhatsappAccess (create) failed:", waErr);
      }
      try {
        await applyGaAccess(supabaseClient, authData.user.id, ga_access);
        await applyMetaAccess(supabaseClient, authData.user.id, meta_access);
      } catch (accErr) {
        console.error("applyGa/MetaAccess (create) failed:", accErr);
      }

      return new Response(JSON.stringify(profileData), {
        headers: { ...corsHeaders, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        status: 200,
      });
    }

    if (action === "update") {
      // Same rule as create: only the backup_root caller may set backup_admin;
      // backup_root itself is never accepted from the client.
      const { email, password, whatsapp_access, ga_access, meta_access, backup_admin, backup_root: _backupRootIgnored, ...rest } = userData;
      if (me.backup_root === true && typeof backup_admin === "boolean") {
        rest.backup_admin = backup_admin;
      }

      if (me.role !== "owner") {
        const { data: targetUser } = await supabaseClient
          .from("users").select("role").eq("id", userId).maybeSingle();
        if (targetUser?.role === "business owner" || rest.role === "business owner") {
          return json({ error: BIZ_OWNER_PROTECTED_MSG }, 403);
        }
      }

      // Read the current auth login email so we only touch GoTrue when something
      // actually changed. Forwarding an unchanged email made GoTrue treat every
      // edit (even password-only) as an email change and reject it with 422.
      let currentAuthEmail: string | null = null;
      {
        const { data: cur, error: curErr } = await supabaseClient.auth.admin.getUserById(userId);
        if (curErr) throw friendlyError(curErr);
        currentAuthEmail = cur?.user?.email ?? null;
      }

      const submittedEmail = typeof email === "string" ? email.trim() : "";
      const emailChanged = submittedEmail.length > 0 &&
        submittedEmail.toLowerCase() !== (currentAuthEmail ?? "").toLowerCase();

      const authUpdates: Record<string, unknown> = {};
      if (emailChanged) {
        authUpdates.email = submittedEmail;
        authUpdates.email_confirm = true; // admin-initiated change, no confirmation round-trip
      }
      if (password) authUpdates.password = password;

      if (Object.keys(authUpdates).length > 0) {
        const { error: authError } = await supabaseClient.auth.admin.updateUserById(
          userId,
          authUpdates,
        );
        if (authError) throw friendlyError(authError, emailChanged ? "email" : "password");
      }

      // auth.users is the source of truth for the login email; the profile email
      // always mirrors it. This both prevents and self-heals drift on every edit.
      const canonicalEmail = emailChanged ? submittedEmail : currentAuthEmail;
      const profilePatch: Record<string, unknown> = { ...rest };
      if (canonicalEmail) profilePatch.email = canonicalEmail;

      const { data: profileData, error: profileError } = await supabaseClient
        .from("users")
        .update(profilePatch)
        .eq("id", userId)
        .select()
        .single();

      if (profileError) throw friendlyError(profileError);

      try {
        await applyWhatsappAccess(supabaseClient, userId, whatsapp_access);
      } catch (waErr) {
        console.error("applyWhatsappAccess (update) failed:", waErr);
      }
      try {
        await applyGaAccess(supabaseClient, userId, ga_access);
        await applyMetaAccess(supabaseClient, userId, meta_access);
      } catch (accErr) {
        console.error("applyGa/MetaAccess (update) failed:", accErr);
      }

      return new Response(JSON.stringify(profileData), {
        headers: { ...corsHeaders, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        status: 200,
      });
    }

    if (action === "delete") {
      // Capture identity BEFORE deletion so the notice can be emailed afterwards.
      const { data: doomed } = await supabaseClient
        .from("users").select('name, email, role, "DigiCom Business"').eq("id", userId).maybeSingle();

      if (doomed?.role === "business owner" && me.role !== "owner") {
        return json({ error: BIZ_OWNER_PROTECTED_MSG }, 403);
      }

      const { error: authError } = await supabaseClient.auth.admin.deleteUser(userId);
      if (authError) throw authError;

      const { error: profileError } = await supabaseClient
        .from("users")
        .delete()
        .eq("id", userId);

      if (profileError) throw profileError;

      // Best-effort "Compte supprimé" email — never affects the deletion result.
      try {
        if (doomed?.email) {
          const ROLE_FR: Record<string, string> = {
            "super admin": "Super administrateur", "business owner": "Propriétaire d'entreprise", "admin": "Administrateur", "commercial": "Commercial",
            "courier": "Livreur", "mediabuyer": "Media buyer", "owner": "Propriétaire",
          };
          let businessName = "votre entreprise";
          if (doomed["DigiCom Business"]) {
            const { data: biz } = await supabaseClient.from("businesses").select("name").eq("id", doomed["DigiCom Business"]).maybeSingle();
            if (biz?.name) businessName = biz.name;
          }
          const nowFr = (() => {
            try { return new Date().toLocaleString("fr-FR", { timeZone: "Africa/Casablanca", dateStyle: "long", timeStyle: "short" }); }
            catch { return new Date().toISOString(); }
          })();
          const SERVICE = Deno.env.get("SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY") ?? "";
          await fetch(`${Deno.env.get("SUPABASE_URL")}/functions/v1/send-email`, {
            method: "POST",
            headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", "Authorization": `Bearer ${SERVICE}`, "apikey": SERVICE },
            body: JSON.stringify({
              key: "account_deleted", to: doomed.email,
              vars: {
                user_name: doomed.name || "",
                role_label: ROLE_FR[doomed.role] || String(doomed.role || ""),
                business_name: businessName,
                deleted_at: nowFr,
              },
            }),
          });
        }
      } catch (e) {
        console.error("account_deleted email failed:", e);
      }

      return new Response(JSON.stringify({ success: true }), {
        headers: { ...corsHeaders, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        status: 200,
      });
    }

    return new Response(JSON.stringify({ error: "Invalid action" }), {
      headers: { ...corsHeaders, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      status: 400,
    });
  } catch (error) {
    return new Response(JSON.stringify({ error: (error as Error).message }), {
      headers: { ...corsHeaders, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      status: 400,
    });
  }
});

          const ROLE_FR: Record<string, string> = {
            "super admin": "Super administrateur", "business owner": "Propriétaire d'entreprise", "admin": "Administrateur", "commercial": "Commercial",
            "courier": "Livreur", "mediabuyer": "Media buyer", "owner": "Propriétaire",
          };
          let businessName = "votre entreprise";
          if (doomed["DigiCom Business"]) {
            const { data: biz } = await supabaseClient.from("businesses").select("name").eq("id", doomed["DigiCom Business"]).maybeSingle();
            if (biz?.name) businessName = biz.name;
          }
          const nowFr = (() => {
            try { return new Date().toLocaleString("fr-FR", { timeZone: "Africa/Casablanca", dateStyle: "long", timeStyle: "short" }); }
            catch { return new Date().toISOString(); }
          })();
          const SERVICE = Deno.env.get("SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY") ?? "";
          await fetch(`${Deno.env.get("SUPABASE_URL")}/functions/v1/send-email`, {
            method: "POST",
            headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", "Authorization": `Bearer ${SERVICE}`, "apikey": SERVICE },
            body: JSON.stringify({
              key: "account_deleted", to: doomed.email,
              vars: {
                user_name: doomed.name || "",
                role_label: ROLE_FR[doomed.role] || String(doomed.role || ""),
                business_name: businessName,
                deleted_at: nowFr,
              },
            }),
          });
        }
      } catch (e) {
        console.error("account_deleted email failed:", e);
      }

      return new Response(JSON.stringify({ success: true }), {
        headers: { ...corsHeaders, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        status: 200,
      });
    }

    return new Response(JSON.stringify({ error: "Invalid action" }), {
      headers: { ...corsHeaders, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      status: 400,
    });
  } catch (error) {
    return new Response(JSON.stringify({ error: (error as Error).message }), {
      headers: { ...corsHeaders, "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      status: 400,
    });
  }
});

To create a publication, the invoking user must have the `CREATE` privilege for the current database. ... `CREATE PUBLICATION` is a PostgreSQL extension.\n\nCREATE PUBLICATION\n---\nPrev   | Up  | SQL Commands  | Home  |  Next\n\n* * *\n\n## CREATE PUBLICATION\n\nCREATE PUBLICATION — define a new publication\n\n## Synopsis\n    \n    CREATE PUBLICATION `name`\n        [ FOR ALL TABLES\n          | FOR `publication_object` [, ... ] ]\n        [ WITH ( `publication_parameter` [= `value`] [, ... ] ) ]\n    \n    where `publication_object` is one of:\n    \n        TABLE `table_and_columns` [, ... ]\n        TABLES IN SCHEMA { `schema_name` | CURRENT_SCHEMA } [, ... ]\n    \n    and `table_and_columns` is:\n    \n        [ ONLY ] `table_name` [ * ] [ ( `column_name` [, ... ] ) ] [ WHERE ( `expression` ) ]\n    \n\n## Description\n\n`CREATE PUBLICATION` adds a new publication into the current database. The publication name must be distinct from the name of any existing publication in the current database.\n\nA publication is essentially a group of tables whose data changes are intended to be replicated through logical replication. See Section 29.1 for details about how publications fit into the logical replication setup.\n\n## Parameters\n\n`name` #\n    \n\nThe name of the new publication.\n\n`FOR TABLE` #\n    \n\nSpecifies a list of tables to add to the publication. If `ONLY` is specified before the table name, only that table is added to the publication. If `ONLY` is not specified, the table and all its descendant tables (if any) are added. Optionally, `*` can be specified after the table name to explicitly indicate that descendant tables are included. This does not apply to a partitioned table, however. The partitions of a partitioned table are always implicitly considered part of the publication, so they are never explicitly added to the publication.\n\nIf the optional `WHERE` clause is specified, it defines a row filter expression. Rows for which the `expression` evaluates to false or null will not be published. Note that parentheses are required around the expression. It has no effect on `TRUNCATE` commands.\n\nWhen a column list is specified, only the named columns are replicated. The column list can contain stored generated columns as well. If the column list is omitted, the publication will replicate all non-generated columns (including any added in the future) by default. Stored generated columns can also be replicated if `publish_generated_columns` is set to `stored`. Specifying a column list has no effect on `TRUNCATE` commands. See Section 29.5 for details about column lists.\n\nOnly persistent base tables and partitioned tables can be part of a publication. Temporary tables, unlogged tables, foreign tables, materialized views, and regular views cannot be part of a publication.\n\nSpecifying a column list when the publication also publishes `FOR TABLES IN SCHEMA` is not supported.\n\nWhen a partitioned table is added to a publication, all of its existing and future partitions are implicitly considered to be part of the publication. So, even operations that are performed directly on a partition are also published via publications that its ancestors are part of.\n\n`FOR ALL TABLES` #\n    \n\nMarks the publication as one that replicates changes for all tables in the database, including tables created in the future.\n\n`FOR TABLES IN SCHEMA` #\n    \n\nMarks the publication as one that replicates changes for all tables in the specified list of schemas, including tables created in the future.\n\nSpecifying a schema when the publication also publishes a table with a column list is not supported.\n\nOnly persistent base tables and partitioned tables present in the schema will be included as part of the publication. Temporary tables, unlogged tables, foreign tables, materialized views, and regular views from the schema will not be part of the publication.\n\nWhen a partitioned table is published via a schema-level publication, all of its existing and future partitions are implicitly considered to be part of the publication, regardless of whether they are from the publication schema or not. So, even operations that are performed directly on a partition are also published via publications that its ancestors are part of.\n\n`WITH ( `publication_parameter` [= `value`] [, ... ] )` #\n    \n\nThis clause specifies optional parameters for a publication. The following parameters are supported:\n\n`publish` (`string`) #\n    \n\nThis parameter determines which DML operations will be published by the new publication to the subscribers. The value is a comma-separated list of operations. The allowed operations are `insert`, `update`, `delete`, and `truncate`. The default is to publish all actions, and so the default value for this option is `'insert, update, delete, truncate'`.\n\nThis parameter only affects DML operations. In particular, the initial data synchronization (see Section 29.9.1) for logical replication does not take this parameter into account when copying existing table data.\n\n`publish_generated_columns` (`enum`) #\n    \n\nSpecifies whether the generated columns present in the tables associated with the publication should be replicated. Possible values are `none` and `stored`.\n\nThe default is `none` meaning the generated columns present in the tables associated with publication will not be replicated.\n\nIf set to `stored`, the stored generated columns present in the tables associated with publication will be replicated.\n## Notes\n\nIf `FOR TABLE`, `FOR ALL TABLES` or `FOR TABLES IN SCHEMA` are not specified, then the publication starts out with an empty set of tables. That is useful if tables or schemas are to be added later.\n\nThe creation of a publication does not start replication. It only defines a grouping and filtering logic for future subscribers.\n\nTo create a publication, the invoking user must have the `CREATE` privilege for the current database. (Of course, superusers bypass this check.)\n\nTo add a table to a publication, the invoking user must have ownership rights on the table. The `FOR ALL TABLES` and `FOR TABLES IN SCHEMA` clauses require the invoking user to be a superuser.\n\nThe tables added to a publication that publishes `UPDATE` and/or `DELETE` operations must have `REPLICA IDENTITY` defined. Otherwise those operations will be disallowed on those tables.\n\nAny column list must include the `REPLICA IDENTITY` columns in order for `UPDATE` or `DELETE` operations to be published. There are no column list restrictions if the publication publishes only `INSERT` operations.\n## Examples\n\nCreate a publication that publishes all changes in two tables:\n    \n    CREATE PUBLICATION mypublication FOR TABLE users, departments;\n    \n\nCreate a publication that publishes all changes from active departments:\n    \n    CREATE PUBLICATION active_departments FOR TABLE departments WHERE (active IS TRUE);\n    \n\nCreate a publication that publishes all changes in all tables:\n    \n    CREATE PUBLICATION alltables FOR ALL TABLES;\n    \n\nCreate a publication that only publishes `INSERT` operations in one table:\n    \n    CREATE PUBLICATION insert_only FOR TABLE mydata\n        WITH (publish = 'insert');\n    \n\nCreate a publication that publishes all changes for tables `users`, `departments` and all changes for all the tables present in the schema `production`:\n    \n    CREATE PUBLICATION production_publication FOR TABLE users, departments, TABLES IN SCHEMA production;\n    \n\nCreate a publication that publishes all changes for all the tables present in the schemas `marketing` and `sales`:\n    \n    CREATE PUBLICATION sales_publication FOR TABLES IN SCHEMA marketing, sales;\n    \n\nCreate a publication that publishes all changes for table `users`, but replicates only columns `user_id` and `firstname`:\n    \n    CREATE PUBLICATION users_filtered FOR TABLE users (user_id, firstname);\n    \n\n## Compatibility\n\n`CREATE PUBLICATION` is a PostgreSQL extension.\n\n## See Also\n\nALTER PUBLICATION, DROP PUBLICATION, CREATE SUBSCRIPTION, ALTER SUBSCRIPTION\n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------\nPostgreSQL: Documentation: 17: 5.9. Row Security Policies (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/ddl-rowsecurity.html)\nciteturn0search1 [wordlim: 200] Published: last week; Crawled: 5 days ago; Operations that apply to the whole table, such as `TRUNCATE` and `REFERENCES`, are not subject to row security. ... In the examples above, the policy expressions consider only the current values in the row to be accessed or updated.\n\n5.9. Row Security Policies\n---\nPrev   | Up  | Chapter 5. Data Definition  | Home  |  Next\n\n* * *\n\n## 5.9. Row Security Policies #\n\nIn addition to the SQL-standard privilege system available through GRANT, tables can have row security policies that restrict, on a per-user basis, which rows can be returned by normal queries or inserted, updated, or deleted by data modification commands. This feature is also known as Row-Level Security. By default, tables do not have any policies, so that if a user has access privileges to a table according to the SQL privilege system, all rows within it are equally available for querying or updating.\n\nWhen row security is enabled on a table (with ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY), all normal access to the table for selecting rows or modifying rows must be allowed by a row security policy. (However, the table's owner is typically not subject to row security policies.) If no policy exists for the table, a default-deny policy is used, meaning that no rows are visible or can be modified. Operations that apply to the whole table, such as `TRUNCATE` and `REFERENCES`, are not subject to row security.\n\nRow security policies can be specific to commands, or to roles, or to both. A policy can be specified to apply to `ALL` commands, or to `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, or `DELETE`. Multiple roles can be assigned to a given policy, and normal role membership and inheritance rules apply.\n\nTo specify which rows are visible or modifiable according to a policy, an expression is required that returns a Boolean result. This expression will be evaluated for each row prior to any conditions or functions coming from the user's query. (The only exceptions to this rule are `leakproof` functions, which are guaranteed to not leak information; the optimizer may choose to apply such functions ahead of the row-security check.) Rows for which the expression does not return `true` will not be processed. Separate expressions may be specified to provide independent control over the rows which are visible and the rows which are allowed to be modified. Policy expressions are run as part of the query and with the privileges of the user running the query, although security-definer functions can be used to access data not available to the calling user.\n\nSuperusers and roles with the `BYPASSRLS` attribute always bypass the row security system when accessing a table. Table owners normally bypass row security as well, though a table owner can choose to be subject to row security with ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY.\n\nEnabling and disabling row security, as well as adding policies to a table, is always the privilege of the table owner only.\n\nPolicies are created using the CREATE POLICY command, altered using the ALTER POLICY command, and dropped using the DROP POLICY command. To enable and disable row security for a given table, use the ALTER TABLE command.\n\nEach policy has a name and multiple policies can be defined for a table. As policies are table-specific, each policy for a table must have a unique name. Different tables may have policies with the same name.\n\nWhen multiple policies apply to a given query, they are combined using either `OR` (for permissive policies, which are the default) or using `AND` (for restrictive policies). In a `SELECT` command, these two policies are combined using `OR`, with the net effect being that all rows can be selected. In other command types, only the second policy applies, so that the effects are the same as before.\n\nRow security can also be disabled with the `ALTER TABLE` command. Disabling row security does not remove any policies that are defined on the table; they are simply ignored. Then all rows in the table are visible and modifiable, subject to the standard SQL privileges system.\n\nBelow is a larger example of how this feature can be used in production environments. The table `passwd` emulates a Unix password file:\n    \n    -- Simple passwd-file based example\n    CREATE TABLE passwd (\n      user_name             text UNIQUE NOT NULL,\n      pwhash                text,\n      uid                   int  PRIMARY KEY,\n      gid                   int  NOT NULL,\n      real_name             text NOT NULL,\n      home_phone            text,\n      extra_info            text,\n      home_dir              text NOT NULL,\n     127.0.0.1\n    (1 row)\n    \n    => TABLE passwd;\n     user_name | pwhash | uid | gid | real_name | home_phone | extra_info | home_dir | shell\n    -----------+--------+-----+-----+-----------+------------+------------+----------+-------\n    (0 rows)\n    \n    => UPDATE passwd set pwhash = NULL;\n    UPDATE 0\n    \n\nReferential integrity checks, such as unique or primary key constraints and foreign key references, always bypass row security to ensure that data integrity is maintained. Care must be taken when developing schemas and row level policies to avoid “covert channel” leaks of information through such referential integrity checks.\n\nIn some contexts it is important to be sure that row security is not being applied. For example, when taking a backup, it could be disastrous if row security silently caused some rows to be omitted from the backup. In such a situation, you can set the row_security configuration parameter to `off`. This does not in itself bypass row security; what it does is throw an error if any query's results would get filtered by a policy. The reason for the error can then be investigated and fixed.\n\nIn the examples above, the policy expressions consider only the current values in the row to be accessed or updated. This is the simplest and best-performing case; when possible, it's best to design row security applications to work this way. If it is necessary to consult other rows or other tables to make a policy decision, that can be accomplished using sub-`SELECT`s, or functions that contain `SELECT`s, in the policy expressions. Be aware however that such accesses can create race conditions that could allow information leakage if care is not taken. As an example, consider the following table design:\n    \n    -- definition of privilege groups\n    CREATE TABLE groups (group_id int PRIMARY KEY,\n                         group_name text NOT NULL);\n    \n    INSERT INTO groups VALUES\n      (1, 'low'),\n      (2, 'medium'),\n      (5, 'high');\n    \n    GRANT ALL ON groups TO alice;  -- alice is the administrator\n    GRANT SELECT ON groups TO public;\n    \n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------\nPostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 52.40. pg_publication (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/catalog-pg-publication.html)\nciteturn0search2 [wordlim: 200] Published: last week; Crawled: yesterday; Table 52.40. `pg_publication` Columns ... `puballtables` `bool` If true, this publication automatically includes all tables in the database, including any that will be created in the future.`pubinsert` `bool` If true, INSERT operations are replicated for tables in the publication.\n\n52.40. `pg_publication`\n---\nPrev   | Up  | Chapter 52. System Catalogs  | Home  |  Next\n\n* * *\n\n## 52.40. `pg_publication` #\n\nThe catalog `pg_publication` contains all publications created in the database. A policy includes the kind of command that it applies to (possibly all commands), the roles that it applies to, the expression to be added as a security-barrier qualification to queries that include the table, and the expression to be added as a `WITH CHECK` option for queries that attempt to add new records to the table.\n\nTable 52.38. `pg_policy` Columns\n\nColumn Type Description\n---\n`oid` `oid` Row identifier\n`polname` `name` The name of the policy\n`polrelid` `oid` (references `pg_class`.`oid`) The table to which the policy applies\n`polcmd` `char` The command type to which the policy is applied: `r` for SELECT, `a` for INSERT, `w` for UPDATE, `d` for DELETE, or `*` for all\n`polpermissive` `bool` Is the policy permissive or restrictive?\n`polroles` `oid[]` (references `pg_authid`.`oid`) The roles to which the policy is applied; zero means `PUBLIC` (and normally appears alone in the array)\n`polqual` `pg_node_tree` The expression tree to be added to the security barrier qualifications for queries that use the table\n`polwithcheck` `pg_node_tree` The expression tree to be added to the WITH CHECK qualifications for queries that attempt to add rows to the table\n\n### Note\n\nPolicies stored in `pg_policy` are applied only when `pg_class`.`relrowsecurity` is set for their table.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------\nPostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: CREATE POLICY (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createpolicy.html)\nciteturn0search4 [wordlim: 200] Published: last week; Note that row-level security must be enabled on the table (using `ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`) in order for created policies to be applied.\n\nA policy grants the permission to select, insert, update, or delete rows that match the relevant policy expression. Existing table rows are checked against the expression specified in `USING`, while new rows that would be created via `INSERT` or `UPDATE` are checked against the expression specified in `WITH CHECK`. When a `USING` expression returns true for a given row then that row is visible to the user, while if false or null is returned then the row is not visible. If only restrictive policies exist, then no records will be accessible. When a mix of permissive and restrictive policies are present, a record is only accessible if at least one of the permissive policies passes, in addition to all the restrictive policies.\n\n`command`\n    \n\nThe command to which the policy applies. Valid options are `ALL`, `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE`. `ALL` is the default. See below for specifics regarding how these are applied.\n\n`role_name`\n    \n\nThe role(s) to which the policy is to be applied. The default is `PUBLIC`, which will apply the policy to all roles.\n\n`using_expression`\n    \n\nAny SQL conditional expression (returning `boolean`). The conditional expression cannot contain any aggregate or window functions. This expression will be added to queries that refer to the table if row-level security is enabled. Rows for which the expression returns true will be visible. Any rows for which the expression returns false or null will not be visible to the user (in a `SELECT`), and will not be available for modification (in an `UPDATE` or `DELETE`). Typically, such rows are silently suppressed; no error is reported (but see Table 300 for exceptions).\n\n`check_expression`\n    \n\nAny SQL conditional expression (returning `boolean`). The conditional expression cannot contain any aggregate or window functions. This expression will be used in `INSERT` and `UPDATE` queries against the table if row-level security is enabled. Only rows for which the expression evaluates to true will be allowed. An error will be thrown if the expression evaluates to false or null for any of the records inserted or any of the records that result from the update. Note that the `check_expression` is evaluated against the proposed new contents of the row, not the original contents.\n\n\nGenerally, the system will enforce filter conditions imposed using security policies prior to qualifications that appear in user queries, in order to prevent inadvertent exposure of the protected data to user-defined functions which might not be trustworthy. However, functions and operators marked by the system (or the system administrator) as `LEAKPROOF` may be evaluated before policy expressions, as they are assumed to be trustworthy.\n\nSince policy expressions are added to the user's query directly, they will be run with the rights of the user running the overall query. Therefore, users who are using a given policy must be able to access any tables or functions referenced in the expression or they will simply receive a permission denied error when attempting to query the table that has row-level security enabled. This does not change how views work, however. As with normal queries and views, permission checks and policies for the tables which are referenced by a view will use the view owner's rights and any policies which apply to the view owner, except if the view is defined using the `security_invoker` option (see `CREATE VIEW`).\n\nNo separate policy exists for `MERGE`. Instead, the policies defined for `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` are applied while executing `MERGE`, depending on the actions that are performed.\n\nAdditional discussion and practical examples can be found in Section 5.9.\n\n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------\nRow-security - PostgreSQL wiki (https://wiki.postgresql.org/wiki/Row-security)\nciteturn0search5 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: last week; PostgreSQL has several SQL commands that allow users to directly access database rows: ... Row-security extensions that inject policy at the C level may choose to ignore `OVERRIDE ROW SECURITY`; they're considered to be trusted. (There is not currently a database privilege named `OVERRIDE ROW SECURITY`, it's implicit, but such a `GRANT`able right should be added in future).\n\nOnly users with `SET ROW SECURITY` rights may apply row security rights to a table. The table owner or the superuser may set row security on a table. Like `OVERRIDE ROW SECURITY` this is currently an implicit right.\n\nRow-level security does not override existing `GRANT` permissions, it adds a finer grained level of control. For example, setting `ROW SECURITY FOR SELECT` to allow a given user to give rows would only give that user access if the user also has `SELECT` privileges on the column or table in question.\n\n### SQL commands for setting row security\n\nRow-security policy is set by a user with `ROW SECURITY` rights (by default, the table owner and superuser), using the following syntax:\n\n(This segment of the design is still in flux)\n    \n    ALTER TABLE <relname> SET ROW SECURITY FOR <privilege> TO (<expression>);\n    \n    ALTER TABLE <relname> RESET ROW SECURITY FOR <privilege>;\n    \n\n<privilege> can be one of: ALL, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. The initial implementation may only support 'ALL'.\n\n'ALL' would simply define the same policy for all the commands. Later commands which update only a single command would replace the policy for that command only, leaving the policy for the other commands to what was set from the initial 'ALL'. The same goes for a RESET.\n\nIf no row security policy has been set for a given command type (or the security policy has been reset for that command type), no row-level security will apply.\n\n--------------------------------------------------------------------------------\nPostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: 5.8. Privileges (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-priv.html)\nciteturn0search6 [wordlim: 200] Published: last week; Crawled: yesterday; `TRIGGER` # ... `EXECUTE` #Allows calling a function or procedure, including use of any operators that are implemented on top of the function. ... THE TOP 10 THINGS THAT WILL ACTUALLY BACKFIRE\n\nRanked by **probability × severity × irreversibility**. Blunt.\n\n### 1. Netting commission out of collected COD — or shipping a \"wallet\"\n**Loi 103-12 Art 183: 6 months–3 years imprisonment + 100,000–5,000,000 MAD.** The instant COD proceeds hit an iGrowFast account, or commission is netted from collected cash, or a seller can draw down an on-platform balance, you are an **unlicensed établissement de paiement** performing *\"opérations de transfert de fonds\"* as *\"intermédiaire entre le payeur et le fournisseur de biens et services\"*, *à titre de profession habituelle*. **And iGrowFast LLC structurally cannot cure it**: Art 35-2 requires a **société anonyme or SARL** — Moroccan forms. A Wyoming LLC is neither. The cure is a Moroccan subsidiary + BAM capital + business plan + BAM review = **12–24 months, capital-intensive.** Note the severity gap: **3 years vs. 1 year, 5M MAD vs. 400k — this is an order of magnitude worse than the entire data-protection schedule combined.** And **Art 182 makes the marketing copy itself the offence** (3 mo–1 yr + 20k–200k) — a \"wallet\" UI or \"we pay your sellers\" headline is punishable **before a single dirham moves**. Free to comply with today. Catastrophic and unfixable if breached. **This is the item to get right before anything else on this page.**\n\n### 2. The US leg of your own architecture is already illegal in Morocco, and no page fixes it\nThe **USA is absent** from the CNDP adequacy list (Délibération 236-2015 — Germany is on it; the US is not). **iGrowFast LLC's own US-based admin/support access to Moroccan personal data is itself a transfer to a non-adequate state.** Read that again: **the company's American nationality creates the violation.** Being a US entity is a **liability** here, not a shield. Add Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, TikTok, Snap, GA, Meta Ads, Shopify. **No Art 44 derogation is available at scale** — express consent is impossible (the sellers' customers never interact with you), and Art 44-1(d) contract-necessity collapses for AI and ad platforms because those are not *necessary* to execute the sale. Only **Art 44-3** (express, reasoned CNDP authorization) covers it, it is **not self-executing** (SCCs are not an instrument in Morocco), it takes 2 months, and it **presupposes an approved déclaration that does not exist**. **Price this correctly: the fines are not the risk.** Art 60 → 400k MAD (~USD 40k) is noise. The risks are **(i) personal criminal liability of directors** (Art 64 — *\"sans préjudice des peines qui peuvent être appliquées à ses dirigeants\"*), **(ii) a court order to erase the production database** (Art 61), **(iii) CNDP's public naming register** (live since 31 Mar 2023 — see the **TLSCONTACT** precedent: hearing 6 Jan 2023, compliance deadline 28 Feb 2023, Arts 52 and 60 invoked, referral to competent authorities), and **(iv) contamination of your seller base** — who are the Art 2-2(a) controllers with **Moroccan assets to seize**. A CNDP enforcement wave against sellers makes iGrowFast the reason their clients got fined. That kills the company commercially long before any criminal process concludes.\n\n### 3. Launching the marketing site with ad pixels and no consent gate\n**You are currently out of GDPR scope for the thing that actually matters** — Moroccan end-customers are not in the Union, so their names, phones, addresses and order contents are outside GDPR **no matter where you host them** (nationality is irrelevant; **location at the moment of the trigger activity** is what counts). And renting Contabo VPSs does **not** create an establishment — the Directive 95/46 \"use of equipment\" criterion was **deliberately deleted** from the GDPR, and EDPB Example 7 is your fact pattern. **Then you put a Meta Pixel on the homepage and hand it all away.** Art 3(2)(b) monitoring has **no intent requirement** (unlike 3(2)(a)); retargeting on an EU-reachable site *is* monitoring. That single tag triggers: Art 27 EU rep, a **separate** UK rep, the full Art 13 stack — **and Guidelines 05/2021 fn.15 makes YOU the exporter** (*\"personal data disclosed via cookies are… a transmission by the operator of the website\"* — you cannot hide behind \"the user's browser sent it\"). **Multiplied by: no establishment = no one-stop-shop under GDPR, and the OSS never applies to ePrivacy at all.** You face **27 supervisory authorities individually, with no lead-authority shield, and no way to buy one** without an EU establishment that would itself trigger Art 3(1) for everything. This is entirely self-inflicted, entirely preventable, and costs one configuration decision.\n\n### 4. TCPA\n**$500 per message, trebled to $1,500 for willful/knowing, per message, no statutory cap, private right of action, the most-classed statute in the US.** 100,000 non-compliant messages = **$50M–$150M nominal**. \"Willful\" under the Communications Act means **a conscious act, irrespective of intent to violate** — a low bar. The WhatsApp-is-not-a-\"call\" argument is **probably right and completely unadjudicated**: *\"treat this as an argument you would win, not a rule you can build a business on.\"* Any **SMS fallback, OTP, or carrier-network message is squarely in scope**. **The indemnity is worthless** — it is paperwork from a judgment-proof Moroccan micro-seller, and under the FCC's 2013 *DISH Network* ruling a platform that supplies templates, schedules sends, optimizes timing, or auto-triggers messages on order events **looks like the \"maker/initiator\"** and is liable **directly**, plus **vicariously** under agency (actual authority, apparent authority, ratification). **The engineering controls are the defense.** And the **cross-subject-matter revocation prong went live 11 April 2026**: an opt-out on a **delivery notification** must now kill **marketing**. Also live: state **mini-TCPAs** (FL, OK, MD, WA CEMA, NJ), several drafted around **\"text message\"** rather than \"call\" — which **routes around *Steidinger* entirely**. And do not over-read *Steidinger v. Blackstone* (7th Cir., 14 Jul 2026): it kills the **§227(c)(5)** DNC private action for texts **only**; **§227(b)** — where the class-action money is — is untouched, and *Howard v. RNC* (9th Cir., 13 Jan 2026) went the other way. **Live circuit split.** Separately, the **highest-probability** Moroccan trigger in the whole stack sits adjacent: WhatsApp broadcast = **prospection directe** (Art 59) — *\"recipients notice it directly.\"*\n\n### 5. Shipping AI features over customer / WhatsApp content\nFour regimes fire simultaneously. **Morocco Art 12-1(b)**: sending order data and message content to Anthropic/OpenAI is *\"l'utilisation de données à caractère personnel à d'autres fins que celles pour lesquelles elles ont été collectées\"* → **AUTORISATION (F112, 2 months), not a déclaration** — *\"the single most under-appreciated trigger in the stack\"* — plus **Art 54 criminal exposure** (3 mo–1 yr + 20k–200k, doubled). **Shopify PPA**: absolute ban on using Merchant/Customer Data — *\"or enabling third parties to use\"* it — to train, fine-tune or improve any ML/AI system. **Meta Platform Terms**: solely for clients' purposes, **segregated**, no cross-client features. **GDPR Art 28(10)**: *\"if a processor infringes this Regulation by determining the purposes and means of processing, the processor shall be considered to be a controller\"* → you have breached the DPA **and you have no legal basis**. Stacked on top: **Anthropic's DPA hard-codes you as controller** when you are a processor, and **AI Act Art 50(1) disclosure binds from 2 August 2026** — **not delayed by the Digital Omnibus**, whatever the delay headlines said. And **message content will incidentally contain health, religious and political data** — *\"a COD platform processing raw message bodies cannot credibly assert it never touches sensitive data\"* (Art 12-1(a)), on which **there is no Moroccan doctrine at all** (UNCERTAIN).\n\n### 6. Publishing a retention schedule or a rights portal you haven't built\n**Both CPPA orders were mechanism failures, not policy-text failures.** **Todd Snyder — $345,178**: a misconfigured privacy portal silently dropped opt-outs **for 40 days**. **Honda — $632,500**: verification demanded before an opt-out, asymmetric choices, agent friction. **Nomi**: promised an in-store opt-out that never existed — the FTC did not allege Nomi lied about *what* it collected; **it lied about a control it offered.** *\"A 'Do Not Sell' link that doesn't work is worse than no link.\"* The same logic destroys a retention table that your **backups, your R2 media store, your blind-HMAC keyword index, and your AI vendors' logs** quietly contradict — that is simultaneously a **§5 deception** and an **Art 5(2) accountability failure**, and WP260 sets the bar at *\"phrased in a way that allows the data subject to assess, on the basis of his or her own situation, what the retention period will be.\"* **Your `/privacy#retention` table is the single sentence on this website most likely to be false on the day it ships.** Ship the deletion jobs first, then the table.\n\n### 7. Any US-hosting implication, on a site whose servers are in Germany\n**The entire marketing positioning is \"a US company.\"** That makes the US-hosting implication **the highest-probability §5 trap for this specific company** — a reader's default inference, not a claim you have to make. And it is false: VPSs are in **Germany (Contabo)**; the messaging vendor is **EU-hosted**. The precedent is exact and expensive: **GoodRx $1.5M**, **BetterHelp $7.8M**, **Avast $16.5M** (banned from selling browsing data; **$15.3M paid to 103,152 consumers in Dec 2025**) — all policies that **misdescribed data flows and third parties**. Adjacent and equally cheap to prove: calling **30 N Gould St Ste R** — *\"one of the most heavily-used mass registered-agent addresses in the US\"* — \"our headquarters\", or claiming a \"US-based team/support\" that does not exist. **A competitor or a journalist proves that in one search.** And understand the real penalty: **§5 alone carries no first-violation fine** (and after *AMG Capital* (2021) the FTC cannot get equitable monetary relief under §13(b)) — the punishment is an **injunction, a 20-year consent order, deletion and algorithmic disgorgement, and reputational kill.** The 20-year order is the sentence. Fix: **state the German hosting plainly.** *\"The mismatch is only damaging when it looks concealed.\"*\n\n### 8. A WhatsApp logo, a UI clone, or an \"Official Partner\" badge — on the page the Meta reviewer opens while deciding\n**Business Verification is a hard gate before App Review**, and the **website is itself a submitted verification field**. So the reviewer reads your marketing site while deciding whether to trust you. On it, pre-approval, they find: a partner badge you never earned, the WhatsApp glyph you have no licence to display (*\"the guidelines don't grant third parties a general marketing licence to display the logo\"* — the nominative carve-out **explicitly withholds it**), and a pixel-faithful WhatsApp-chrome clone in `#25D366`. That is **the exact \"conveys a relationship that doesn't exist\" pattern**, on the exact page, at the exact moment. Compounding it: **\"built on the WhatsApp Business Platform\" / \"official Cloud API\"** is **false today** because messaging runs through a third-party provider — *\"a reviewer who sees an unapproved applicant already claiming official-API status reads it as either misrepresentation or evidence of unofficial-access use — the latter being an independent basis for denial.\"* And **it costs you nothing commercially to avoid**: build the demo in your own design language — which is what you're actually selling — and say \"Works with WhatsApp\" in text. *\"This is the claim most likely to appear on a founder-written landing page — kill it now.\"* Separately, the same third-party stack is arguably an **Anthropic AUP breach today** (*\"circumvent the guardrails or terms of other platforms\"*) regardless of what the website says.\n\n### 9. Subscription billing without the ROSCA stack\n**Click-to-cancel (16 CFR Part 425) was VACATED IN ITS ENTIRETY by the Eighth Circuit on 8 July 2025 — six days before its compliance date. It never took effect.** Do not read that as safety. The grounds were **procedural** (the FTC skipped the preliminary regulatory analysis after its own ALJ found >$100M impact); **the substantive policy was not repudiated**, and an **ANPRM went to OIRA on 30 January 2026**. Meanwhile **ROSCA (15 U.S.C. §8403) is fully in force** and is the live vehicle: **Amazon — $2.5B** (25 Sep 2025; $1B civil penalty + $1.5B redress to ~35M consumers; **two named executives, an SVP and a VP, personally charged**); **Chegg — $7.5M**; **FTC v. Uber** pending. **All three post-date or bracket the vacatur.** A ROSCA violation is treated as an **FTC rule violation → $53,088 per violation + redress + injunction.** Then **California's ARL** (AB 2863, contracts entered/amended/extended on or after 1 July 2025) adds a remedy that should stop the room: **non-compliant goods are deemed an unconditional gift — full refund of everything ever charged.** And note what Amazon means for the founder-anonymity constraint: **personal liability survives website anonymity.**\n\n### 10. \"Worldwide\" + OFAC — and a sanctions clause copied from a template\niGrowFast LLC is a **US person**. OFAC prohibitions attach **wherever located**, and **liability is STRICT** — *\"'We didn't know the user was in Iran' is not a defense.\"* **IEEPA: greater of ~$377,700 per violation or twice the transaction value; criminal up to $1,000,000 and 20 years.** Morocco is clean; **the \"worldwide\" pitch is what creates the surface** — and it is an adjective, not a strategy. Then the template betrays you: **every ToS on the internet still lists Syria, and that is now affirmatively wrong.** **E.O. 14312** (30 Jun 2025, effective 1 Jul 2025) terminated the national emergency and revoked E.O.s 13338/13399/13460/13572/13573/13582; the **Syrian Sanctions Regulations, 31 CFR Part 542, were REMOVED from the CFR on 26 August 2025.** Publishing a stale embargo list is a false term in your own contract. Equally wrong in the other direction: describing **Russia, Belarus or Venezuela as embargoed** — they are **targeted/sectoral, not territorial**. Correct list: **Cuba, Iran, North Korea + Crimea/DNR/LNR (+Kherson, Zaporizhzhia)**. **Reference the SDN List, not a hand-maintained country list that goes stale.** And the clause is worthless without **T1.9**: screening at signup, periodic re-screening, the **50 Percent Rule**, and a **log** — *\"the record is what mitigates the penalty.\"*\n\n**Honourable mentions that did not make the ten but will still hurt:** Morocco **Art 59 prospection directe** (highest *complaint* probability of anything here); **ADA/Unruh** ($4,000/violation + fees, plaintiff-chosen forum — Wyoming's 10th Circuit does not protect you); the **accessiBe overlay trap** ($1M — never repeat a vendor's compliance claim); **Meta's missing UK DPF extension**; **Shopify PPA §9.14** vs. the core loop; **Woo §1.2.9** vs. commission pricing; **CIN capture** silently escalating every filing.\n\n---\n\n# 5.
