GOOGLE API SERVICES USER DATA POLICY\nSource: https://developers.google.com/terms/api-services-user-data-policy\nWorkspace overlay: https://developers.google.com/workspace/workspace-api-user-data-developer-policy\n\nDISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS (verbatim):\n- \"publish a privacy policy that fully documents how your application interacts with user data\" and list that URL in the OAuth configuration.\n- \"Your Privacy Policy and all in-product privacy notifications should be accurate, comprehensive, and easily accessible.\"\n- Disclosures must be \"prominent and timely.\"\n- Must \"accurately represent\" three things: who requests the data, what data is requested, why it is requested.\n- If data uses expand beyond original disclosures: \"update your privacy policy and prompt the user to consent to any changes.\"\n- Minimum scope: \"Don't request access to information that you don't need. Only request access to the permissions necessary to implement your application's features.\"\n\nLIMITED USE — the four obligations (verbatim):\n(a) \"Limit your use of data to providing or improving user-facing features that are prominent in the requesting application's user interface.\"\n(b) \"Transfers of data are not allowed, except: To provide or improve your appropriate access or user-facing features that are visible and prominent in the requesting application's user interface and only with the user's consent; For security purposes (for example, investigating abuse); To comply with applicable laws; or, As part of a merger, acquisition, or sale of assets of the developer after obtaining explicit prior consent from the user.\"\n(c) \"Don't allow humans to read the data, unless: You first obtained the user's affirmative agreement to view specific messages, files, or other data...; It is necessary for security purposes...; It is necessary to comply with applicable law; or The data (including derivations) is aggregated and used for internal operations in accordance with applicable privacy and other jurisdictional legal requirements.\"\n(d) Prohibited: \"Transferring or selling user data to third parties like advertising platforms, data brokers, or any information resellers\"; \"Transferring, selling, or using user data for serving ads, including retargeting, personalized or interest-based advertising\"; \"Transferring, selling, or using user data to determine credit-worthiness or for lending purposes.\"\n\n*** THE AI/ML QUESTION — DEFINITIVE ANSWER ***\nThe AI/ML clause is REAL and is in the Workspace API User Data and Developer Policy, verbatim:\n\n  \"Transferring, selling, or using user data to create, train, or improve a machine learning or artificial intelligence model beyond that specific user's personalized model for the appropriate use case or user-facing feature.\"\n\n(Note: two independent summarization passes of the base policy page reported \"no AI/ML language exists.\" That is WRONG — the clause lives in the Workspace overlay policy, which is the one that governs Sheets. Anyone researching this who only reads the base policy will reach the wrong conclusion.)\n\nDoes Limited Use prohibit sending Google-user-data to OpenAI/Anthropic? NO — NOT CATEGORICALLY. It draws a hard line between TRAINING and INFERENCE:\n\n- TRAINING on Google user data → PROHIBITED outright, except a model personalized to that specific user for that specific feature. A cross-tenant model trained on many sellers' Sheets data = violation. No consent cures this; it is not one of the enumerated exceptions.\n- INFERENCE (sending data to an LLM to produce output for the user) → this is a \"transfer to a third party\" and is PERMITTED ONLY inside exception (b): the feature must be \"visible and prominent in the requesting application's user interface\" AND have \"the user's consent.\" A background/invisible AI enrichment pass over Sheets data fails the \"prominent in the UI\" test.\n\nTherefore three conditions must ALL hold to send Sheets-sourced data to OpenAI/Anthropic:\n  1. Zero-retention / no-training API tier, contractually confirmed (both OpenAI and Anthropic API defaults do not train on API data; the retention window and abuse-monitoring human review are the exposure).\n  2. The AI feature is prominent and visible in the app UI, not a silent backend process.\n  3. Seller consent is obtained and the privacy policy discloses the AI subprocessor by name.\nCondition (c) \"don't allow humans to read the data\" is the sleeper risk: AI-provider trust-and-safety staff reviewing flagged prompts would breach this. Zero-data-retention endpoints are the mitigation.\n\n*** CRITICAL SCOPING INSIGHT — the escape hatch ***\nLimited Use governs ONLY data obtained THROUGH Google APIs. COD order data that a seller types directly into iGrowFast, or imports by CSV, is NOT Google user data and Limited Use does not touch it at all. Only the Sheets-sync path is constrained. Architecturally: keep AI features on the native data path, and they are entirely outside this policy. If AI must touch Sheets-sourced rows, the three conditions above bind. This distinction is worth designing around — it is the difference between a governed and an ungoverned AI roadmap.\n\nCompliance with this policy is INDEPENDENT of verification status: per https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13464323, all apps must comply with the API Services User Data Policy regardless of whether they are exempt from verification. The Service Account exemption removes the verification process, NOT the Limited Use obligations.\n\n=====================================================================\n2. OAUTH APP VERIFICATION\nSources: https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13463073 ; https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13464321 ; https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/brand-verification\n\nTRIGGER (verbatim): \"Apps that request access to scopes categorized as sensitive or restricted must complete Google's OAuth app verification before being granted access.\" Non-sensitive-only apps are not required to verify (but still need brand verification to show a name/logo on the consent screen). Tier is auto-labelled in the Cloud Console scope picker when you add a scope — the Console is the authoritative tier oracle.\n\nHOMEPAGE (verbatim):\n- \"The homepage must be hosted on a verified domain you own\"\n- \"The homepage must accurately represent and identify your app or brand\"\n- \"The homepage must describe your app's functionality to its users. Your homepage can not be only a login page\"\n- \"publicly accessible, and not just accessible to your site's logged-in users\"\n- Must not be a Google Play Store or Facebook page link\n- \"You must add the link of your privacy policy to your homepage and this link should match the link you added on your OAuth consent screen configuration\"\n\nPRIVACY POLICY (verbatim):\n- \"The Privacy Policy should be hosted within the domain that hosts your homepage\" — SAME DOMAIN AS HOMEPAGE, MANDATORY\n- \"The Privacy Policy should be linked on your homepage so that users can find this information easily\"\n- \"The Privacy Policy must be linked from the OAuth consent screen on the Google API Console\"\n- \"must disclose how your app accesses, uses, stores, and/or shares Google user data\"\n- \"In-product privacy notifications must be prominently displayed in your app interface\"\n\nTERMS OF SERVICE: ToS URL is an authorized-domain-listed URI. Google's brand-verification requirements enumerate homepage, privacy policy, ToS, redirect URIs and JS origins as URIs whose top-level domains must all be listed in Authorized Domains and owned/verified. Google specifies far less normative detail for ToS than for the privacy policy — ToS is not the load-bearing document here. UNCERTAIN whether Google mandates a ToS at all for a non-Marketplace OAuth app; it is required as a field for Marketplace listings.\n\nAPP NAME / LOGO / BRANDING (verbatim):\n- \"All apps that access Google APIs must verify that they accurately represent their identity and intent\"\n- Consent screen must accurately display the app name and logo as configured on the Branding page; \"Any changes require resubmission and approval before taking effect.\"\n- \"Buttons or links that initiate an action on a Google product must follow the Google branding guidelines.\"\n\nDEMO VIDEO (required for sensitive/restricted scopes) (verbatim):\n- \"Show the end-to-end flow of your app including the OAuth grant process\"\n- \"Show the same application you have submitted for verification (including app name, branding)\"\n- \"Show the complete OAuth Consent Screen... The consent screen must also show the same exact scopes you are requesting\"\n- \"Must demonstrate the app functionalities that utilize the requested OAuth scopes\"\nPractical note for iGrowFast: the video must show the OAuth consent screen with matching branding. It does NOT require a founder on camera or any named person — a screen recording satisfies it. The founder-anonymity constraint is compatible with verification.\n\n=====================================================================\n3. SCOPE TIERS\nSource (authoritative, tier-labelled): https://developers.google.com/sheets/api/scopes ; https://developers.google.com/drive/api/guides/api-specific-auth\n\nDefinitions: Non-sensitive = \"provide the smallest scope of authorization access\"; Sensitive = \"provide access to specific Google User Data\"; Restricted = \"provide wide access to Google User Data.\"\n\nGOOGLE SHEETS (confirmed tiers):\n  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets            → SENSITIVE\n  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets.readonly   → SENSITIVE\n  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file              → NON-SENSITIVE  ← recommended\n  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive                   → RESTRICTED     ← triggers CASA\n  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.readonly          → RESTRICTED     ← triggers CASA\n\nGOOGLE DRIVE (confirmed):\n  drive.file, drive.appdata → NON-SENSITIVE (\"recommended for most use cases\", \"per-file access\")\n  drive, drive.readonly, drive.metadata → RESTRICTED\nGoogle explicitly pushes migration to drive.file, which \"grants per-file and narrow access\" and avoids the restricted-scope verification burden.\n\nGOOGLE ANALYTICS (exact strings confirmed; TIER UNCERTAIN):\n  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/analytics\n  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/analytics.readonly\n  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/analytics.edit\n  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/analytics.manage.users\n  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/analytics.manage.users.readonly\n  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/analytics.provision\n  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/analytics.user.deletion\nUNCERTAIN: the OAuth scopes reference page does not render tier markers in fetched form, and I found no official page labelling Analytics scopes. They are NOT on any restricted-scope list I could locate, so they are Sensitive or Non-sensitive — NOT Restricted, therefore NOT CASA-triggering. Confirm the exact label in the Cloud Console scope picker, which auto-labels.\n\nGOOGLE ADS (exact string confirmed; TIER UNCERTAIN):\n  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords\nUNCERTAIN: no official page I fetched labels its tier. Not on any restricted list found → not CASA-triggering. Confirm in Console. Separately, the Google Ads API imposes its OWN gate independent of OAuth verification: a developer token with Basic/Standard access, approved by a Google Ads API application review. That is a distinct process from OAuth verification and applies regardless.\n\n=====================================================================\n4. CASA (Cloud Application Security Assessment)\nSources: https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13465431 ; https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/restricted-scope-verification ; https://appdefensealliance.dev/casa\n\nWHEN REQUIRED (verbatim): \"Every app that requests access to Google users' restricted data and has the ability to access data from or through a third-party server must go through a security assessment.\"\nTIER THAT TRIGGERS IT: RESTRICTED SCOPES ONLY. Sensitive scopes do NOT trigger CASA — they trigger verification (video, homepage, privacy policy) but no security assessment. This is the single most important cost boundary in this whole document.\n\nFRAMEWORK: \"To standardize our security assessment we use the App Defense Alliance and the cloud application security assessment framework (CASA).\" \"CASA utilizes a risk-based, multi-tiered approach\"; apps are assigned \"either the AL1 or AL2 assurance level.\" CASA is \"based 100% on the OWASP ASVS; no proprietary requirements.\" Tier assignment is driven by data sensitivity, number of users per data type, risk tolerance, and risk indicators. \"All requirements must be satisfied for every level, the only difference between each level is the assessment method that applies.\"\n\nWHO PERFORMS IT: independent CASA-authorized labs/assessors accredited by the App Defense Alliance. Google does not perform it.\n\nCOST: Google's own statement (verbatim, https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13463817): \"Google does not charge the developer any fees for security assessment\" and \"The cost for such a service is agreed on between the developer and the assessor without any involvement from Google.\"\nUNCERTAIN — DOLLAR FIGURES: A search-engine synthesis surfaced \"$500 to $4,500 USD\" with \"2-3 weeks for tier-2, 4-6 weeks for tier-3,\" attributed to Google Workspace Marketplace docs. I fetched both Marketplace pages directly (developers.google.com/gsuite/marketplace/security-assessment and /workspace/marketplace/about-app-review) and NEITHER contains those figures — they only say \"If your app uses restricted scopes, it must also go through a security assessment.\" I therefore do NOT assert that range. The older widely-circulated \"$15,000–$75,000\" figure likewise does not appear in current official documentation. TREAT ALL PUBLISHED DOLLAR FIGURES AS UNVERIFIED; the only official position is that price is negotiated bilaterally with the assessor. Get direct quotes from multiple authorized labs.\n\nFREQUENCY (verbatim): \"All applications must be revalidated every year.\" And: \"apps must be reverified for compliance and complete a security assessment at least every 12 months after your assessor's Letter of Assessment (LOA) approval date.\" \"The required assurance level is dynamic and may increase based on changes in your user base or data-handling practices\" — i.e. growth alone can escalate the tier.\nNo free/self-service assessment tier is documented; both AL1 and AL2 are described as lab-tested/lab-verified.\n\nHOW TO AVOID CASA — three independent routes, any one suffices:\n  (i) Never request a restricted scope. Use drive.file (non-sensitive) or spreadsheets (sensitive). CASA is restricted-only.\n  (ii) Use a Service Account and no user OAuth (see §5) — removes the verification surface entirely.\n  (iii) Stay internal-only / under the exemptions in §5.\nFor iGrowFast, (i) and (ii) both already hold. They are not near CASA and should never go near it.\n\n=====================================================================\n5. *** THE CRITICAL ARCHITECTURE QUESTION — SERVICE ACCOUNT ***\nSource: https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13464323 ; https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/restricted-scope-verification ; https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13463817\n\nTHE EXEMPTION, VERBATIM (Google lists five cases where verification is NOT needed):\n  1. \"If the app is for your personal use (fewer than 100 users)\"\n  2. \"Apps in development/testing/staging mode are not subject to verification.\"\n  3. \"The app only accesses its own data (using a Service Account), and not user data (linked to a Google Account).\"\n  4. \"The app is only used by people in your Google Workspace or Cloud Identity organization\" (internal user type)\n  5. Workspace admin-trusted / Marketplace apps: \"An administrator can add a third-party app to the list of trusted apps in the Google Admin console.\"\n\nAnd verbatim from the restricted-scope verification page: \"If your app uses a service account to access only its own data, and it doesn't access any user data (linked to a Google Account), then you don't need to submit for verification.\"\n\nANSWER: YES — the Service Account model avoids OAuth verification and CASA. But the reasoning that makes it robust is MECHANICAL, not merely textual, and the textual exemption is a weaker support than it first appears. Both halves matter:\n\nTHE MECHANICAL ARGUMENT (strong, and the one to rely on):\nOAuth verification is a property of the OAuth CLIENT and its CONSENT SCREEN. A service account authenticates as ITSELF via a signed JWT assertion exchanged for a token bearing the SA's own identity. There is no consent screen, no user OAuth grant, no per-user token. Consequently:\n  - The \"unverified app\" warning screen cannot render — there is no consent screen to prepend it to.\n  - The 100-new-user cap cannot be consumed — that counter increments on user OAuth grants, of which there are zero.\n  - There is no verification submission to make — Google's verification intake is bound to an OAuth consent screen / brand configuration. A product with no consent screen has nothing to submit.\nCASA follows verification. No verification surface → no CASA. This holds regardless of which scopes the SA requests: an SA using the Sensitive `spreadsheets` scope still shows no consent screen, so scope tier is moot in the SA path. Tier only starts mattering the moment a consent screen exists.\n\nTHE TEXTUAL TENSION (be honest about this — it is the residual risk):\nThe exemption says \"accesses its own data ... and NOT user data (linked to a Google Account).\" When a Moroccan seller shares a spreadsheet they OWN with the SA's email, that spreadsheet IS data linked to a Google Account. A literal reading of the exemption is therefore ADVERSE — the SA is a Drive ACL grantee, not the owner. Google's drafting plainly contemplates the canonical case (SA owns/created the resource, e.g. its own BigQuery data), not the shared-file case.\nWeighing it: the mechanical argument dominates in practice — Google has no enforcement mechanism against a consent-screen-less SA, and Google's own FAQ blesses an adjacent shared-resource pattern verbatim: \"You can access data from your users' Google Cloud projects by creating a service account to represent your service, and then having your customers grant that service account appropriate access to their cloud data using IAM policies.\" That is precisely the share-with-the-SA topology, described approvingly. This is the strongest available authority for the pattern.\nVerdict: the SA + user-shared-sheet model does not require verification and does not incur CASA. Confidence: high on the mechanics, moderate on the letter of the exemption. This is not a five-figure annual assessment — it is nothing.\n\nLIMITS OF THE APPROACH — what breaks it:\n  a) DOMAIN-WIDE DELEGATION IS THE TRAP. If the SA is ever given DWD to impersonate users, it IS accessing user data on their behalf and verification applies for sensitive/restricted scopes. DWD is also unusable for iGrowFast's actual users: DWD requires a Google Workspace/Cloud Identity org admin. Sellers on consumer @gmail.com cannot grant it. The manual-share model is not merely acceptable — it is the ONLY option for consumer-Gmail sellers. Fortunate accident: the architecture is forced into the exempt shape.\n  b) ADDING A \"CONNECT YOUR GOOGLE ACCOUNT\" BUTTON destroys the exemption instantly. Per-user OAuth to `spreadsheets` (Sensitive) → full verification: homepage, same-domain privacy policy, demo video, Google review. Still no CASA (Sensitive ≠ Restricted) — unless someone reaches for `drive`/`drive.readonly`, which is Restricted and lands them in annual CASA. Treat a Google-account-connect button as a change requiring explicit sign-off.\n  c) LIMITED USE STILL BINDS. The exemption removes the PROCESS, not the POLICY. §1's AI/ML and transfer rules apply to Sheets-sourced data whether or not verification was ever required.\n  d) UX/OPERATIONAL COST: sellers must manually share each sheet with an unfriendly SA address (…iam.gserviceaccount.com). Support burden, not a compliance one.\n  e) SCOPE MECHANICS: `drive.file` covers only files the app created or the user opened via Picker — it does NOT cover a file manually shared with the SA. For the SA + shared-sheet flow the SA needs `spreadsheets`. Fine (no consent screen), but note this forecloses the \"just use drive.file\" answer IF they ever migrate to per-user OAuth. On that migration path they'd need `spreadsheets` (Sensitive, verification, no CASA) or a Picker-based drive.file flow (Non-sensitive, no verification) — the Picker route is the one to design toward if they ever leave the SA model.\n  f) KEY MANAGEMENT: the SA private key in Postgres Vault is now a crown-jewel credential granting access to every seller sheet ever shared with it. Compromise = cross-tenant breach of end-customer COD data with no per-user revocation granularity (sellers can individually unshare, but there is no token-revocation story). This is the real risk the SA model creates in exchange for the compliance relief. It is a GDPR/security exposure, not a Google-policy one — and given German-hosted infra processing EU-adjacent and Moroccan end-customer PII, it deserves separate attention.\n\n=====================================================================\n6. DOMAIN VERIFICATION\nSource: https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/brand-verification ; https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13464321\n\n- \"You must verify that you own all domains listed in your Authorized domains section.\"\n- Method: \"Verify the ownership of your authorized domains using Google Search Console.\" An account listed as project owner or editor on the GCP project must perform the verification; a Google Account with owner permissions must be associated with the API Console project.\n- Authorized Domains must list the top-level domains of every URI: homepage, privacy policy, ToS, redirect URIs, JavaScript origins.\n\nAPEX vs SUBDOMAIN — DIRECT ANSWER: verifying the apex is sufficient and subdomains need no separate verification. Google requires verification of \"the top private domain\" (the domain available for registration on a public suffix). Google's own example, verbatim: \"an OAuth consent screen that's configured with an application home page of https://sub.example.com/product asks the account holder to verify ownership of the example.com domain.\"\nFor iGrowFast: verify igrowfast.com in Search Console once. That single verification covers app.igrowfast.com and api.igrowfast.com. Homepage on the apex + app on the subdomain is exactly the topology Google's example describes. No conflict.\nFounder-anonymity note: Search Console verification is a private control-proof (DNS TXT record or file upload) between the domain owner and Google. It publishes nothing and requires no public name. DNS TXT is the cleanest method. Compatible with the no-founder-names constraint.\n\n=====================================================================\n7. CONSEQUENCES OF AN UNVERIFIED APP\nSource: https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/7454865 ; https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13463817\n\n- UNVERIFIED APP SCREEN: shown before the consent screen when the app uses sensitive/restricted scopes and has not completed verification.\n- 100-USER CAP (verbatim): \"New user cap\" of \"100 new users in total, after the app presents the unverified app screen.\" And: \"the user cap applies over the entire lifetime of the project, and it cannot be reset or changed.\" This is lifetime and permanent — not a rolling or resettable quota. Burning it on testing is unrecoverable without a new GCP project.\n- HARD FAILURE (verbatim): \"Failure to get your app verified before making requests to sensitive or restricted scopes will result in your project's 100 new-user cap eventually getting exhausted and Google sign-in being disabled for your users.\"\n- ADDITIONAL SIGNALS: Google Security Checkup flags the app as \"risky and unverified\"; users get notices about potential loss of functionality.\n- GRACE PERIOD: exists only in one narrow case — when Google RECLASSIFIES a scope as sensitive/restricted, existing apps get \"a grace period to go through verification before the unverified app screen and user cap are applied.\" There is no general grace period for new apps.\n- RESTRICTED SCOPES: not described as an instant hard block; they route through the same warning + cap mechanism, plus the mandatory security assessment before verification can complete.\n- Testing/dev is explicitly fine unverified: you can \"continue to build and test your app while waiting to complete verification.\"\n\nALL OF §7 IS INAPPLICABLE TO THE SA PATH — these consequences attach to the OAuth consent screen, which the SA architecture does not have. §7 is the description of what iGrowFast is avoiding, and the reason to keep avoiding it.\n\n=====================================================================\nNET ASSESSMENT FOR iGrowFast\n- Today, on the Service Account model: NO OAuth verification, NO CASA, NO 100-user cap, NO demo video. Zero Google review exposure.\n- The website requirements (homepage, same-domain privacy policy, Search Console verification) are NOT currently mandatory for Google, because nothing triggers verification. Build them anyway — they are cheap, they are required by GDPR/Moroccan reality independent of Google, and they are the prerequisite that must already exist on the day anyone proposes a Google-account-connect button. Retrofitting them under deadline is where projects fail.\n- The live, binding Google obligation today is LIMITED USE on Sheets-sourced data — specifically the prohibition on training AI/ML models on it. This constrains the AI roadmap NOW, with no verification trigger and no warning shot.\n- Highest-leverage decisions: (1) never request drive/drive.readonly; (2) never add per-user OAuth without deliberate sign-off; (3) never enable domain-wide delegation; (4) keep AI features on the native (non-Sheets) data path where Limited Use does not reach; (5) treat the SA key as the cross-tenant crown jewel it now is.\n- Two open items: exact Console tier labels for analytics/adwords scopes (confirm in the Cloud Console scope picker — it auto-labels), and real CASA pricing (only if they ever go restricted, which they should not).",

-- TKT-10 backfill: each existing business's EARLIEST super admin becomes its
-- business owner. Rule + the exact 7-user list previewed to and approved by
-- the owner 2026-07-29 (Bellora Bio, El Moda, Golden Design, moulay soltan,
-- Orelle, Ouzlim Bio, test env). Runs AFTER 20260729150000 (trigger + unique
-- index exist; the trigger only guards demotion/deletion, not promotion, and
-- the partial unique index enforces one owner per business).

BEGIN;
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '5s';

UPDATE public.users u
SET role = 'business owner'
FROM (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (u2."DigiCom Business") u2.id
    FROM public.users u2
    WHERE u2.role = 'super admin' AND u2."DigiCom Business" IS NOT NULL
    ORDER BY u2."DigiCom Business", u2.created_at ASC
) first_admin
WHERE u.id = first_admin.id;

COMMIT;
COMMIT;

329:  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions bypass RLS.** A `SECURITY DEFINER` function runs with its creator's privileges — typically a role with `bypassrls` (e.g., `postgres`). Never add `SECURITY DEFINER` to resolve a permission error; it silently removes access control without fixing the underlying cause. Prefer `SECURITY INVOKER`.
330:  - **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions in `public` are callable by all roles.** Postgres grants `EXECUTE` to `PUBLIC` by default for every new function, so any `SECURITY DEFINER` function in `public` is a public API endpoint callable by `anon` and `authenticated` (which inherit from `PUBLIC`) without any additional grant. When `SECURITY DEFINER` is genuinely needed (e.g., bypassing RLS on an internal lookup table), keep the function in a non-exposed schema, always include an `auth.uid()` check in the function body, and run `supabase db advisors` after making changes.

4793:   The 44 `ALTER POLICY` statements cover 16 tables and appear before roughly 140 KB of function/index/trigger/view work. PostgreSQL implements `ALTER POLICY` with `AccessExclusiveLock`, held until transaction end. `lock_timeout = '5s'` limits acquisition waits, not the time already-acquired locks block reads and writes. A later contested lock can therefore block previously locked tables for up to five seconds before rollback. [PostgreSQL policy implementation](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/master/src/backend/commands/policy.c).  
4797:   Direct `UPDATE users SET role=...` fires correctly, and FK-cascaded deletes fire the row-level DELETE trigger. But an earlier `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger can modify `NEW.role` during an update whose target list omitted `role`; PostgreSQL explicitly says column-specific triggers do not fire for such changes. No current repo trigger was found that mutates the role this way. [PostgreSQL trigger behavior](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createtrigger.html).

THE TOP 10 THINGS THAT WILL ACTUALLY BACKFIRE\n\nRanked by **probability × severity × irreversibility**. Blunt.\n\n### 1. Netting commission out of collected COD — or shipping a \"wallet\"\n**Loi 103-12 Art 183: 6 months–3 years imprisonment + 100,000–5,000,000 MAD.** The instant COD proceeds hit an iGrowFast account, or commission is netted from collected cash, or a seller can draw down an on-platform balance, you are an **unlicensed établissement de paiement** performing *\"opérations de transfert de fonds\"* as *\"intermédiaire entre le payeur et le fournisseur de biens et services\"*, *à titre de profession habituelle*. **And iGrowFast LLC structurally cannot cure it**: Art 35-2 requires a **société anonyme or SARL** — Moroccan forms. A Wyoming LLC is neither. The cure is a Moroccan subsidiary + BAM capital + business plan + BAM review = **12–24 months, capital-intensive.** Note the severity gap: **3 years vs. 1 year, 5M MAD vs. 400k — this is an order of magnitude worse than the entire data-protection schedule combined.** And **Art 182 makes the marketing copy itself the offence** (3 mo–1 yr + 20k–200k) — a \"wallet\" UI or \"we pay your sellers\" headline is punishable **before a single dirham moves**. Free to comply with today. Catastrophic and unfixable if breached. **This is the item to get right before anything else on this page.**\n\n### 2. The US leg of your own architecture is already illegal in Morocco, and no page fixes it\nThe **USA is absent** from the CNDP adequacy list (Délibération 236-2015 — Germany is on it; the US is not). **iGrowFast LLC's own US-based admin/support access to Moroccan personal data is itself a transfer to a non-adequate state.** Read that again: **the company's American nationality creates the violation.** Being a US entity is a **liability** here, not a shield. Add Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, TikTok, Snap, GA, Meta Ads, Shopify. **No Art 44 derogation is available at scale** — express consent is impossible (the sellers' customers never interact with you), and Art 44-1(d) contract-necessity collapses for AI and ad platforms because those are not *necessary* to execute the sale. Only **Art 44-3** (express, reasoned CNDP authorization) covers it, it is **not self-executing** (SCCs are not an instrument in Morocco), it takes 2 months, and it **presupposes an approved déclaration that does not exist**. **Price this correctly: the fines are not the risk.** Art 60 → 400k MAD (~USD 40k) is noise. The risks are **(i) personal criminal liability of directors** (Art 64 — *\"sans préjudice des peines qui peuvent être appliquées à ses dirigeants\"*), **(ii) a court order to erase the production database** (Art 61), **(iii) CNDP's public naming register** (live since 31 Mar 2023 — see the **TLSCONTACT** precedent: hearing 6 Jan 2023, compliance deadline 28 Feb 2023, Arts 52 and 60 invoked, referral to competent authorities), and **(iv) contamination of your seller base** — who are the Art 2-2(a) controllers with **Moroccan assets to seize**. A CNDP enforcement wave against sellers makes iGrowFast the reason their clients got fined. That kills the company commercially long before any criminal process concludes.\n\n### 3. Launching the marketing site with ad pixels and no consent gate\n**You are currently out of GDPR scope for the thing that actually matters** — Moroccan end-customers are not in the Union, so their names, phones, addresses and order contents are outside GDPR **no matter where you host them** (nationality is irrelevant; **location at the moment of the trigger activity** is what counts). And renting Contabo VPSs does **not** create an establishment — the Directive 95/46 \"use of equipment\" criterion was **deliberately deleted** from the GDPR, and EDPB Example 7 is your fact pattern. **Then you put a Meta Pixel on the homepage and hand it all away.** Art 3(2)(b) monitoring has **no intent requirement** (unlike 3(2)(a)); retargeting on an EU-reachable site *is* monitoring. That single tag triggers: Art 27 EU rep, a **separate** UK rep, the full Art 13 stack — **and Guidelines 05/2021 fn.15 makes YOU the exporter** (*\"personal data disclosed via cookies are… a transmission by the operator of the website\"* — you cannot hide behind \"the user's browser sent it\"). **Multiplied by: no establishment = no one-stop-shop under GDPR, and the OSS never applies to ePrivacy at all.** You face **27 supervisory authorities individually, with no lead-authority shield, and no way to buy one** without an EU establishment that would itself trigger Art 3(1) for everything. This is entirely self-inflicted, entirely preventable, and costs one configuration decision.\n\n### 4. TCPA\n**$500 per message, trebled to $1,500 for willful/knowing, per message, no statutory cap, private right of action, the most-classed statute in the US.** 100,000 non-compliant messages = **$50M–$150M nominal**. \"Willful\" under the Communications Act means **a conscious act, irrespective of intent to violate** — a low bar. The WhatsApp-is-not-a-\"call\" argument is **probably right and completely unadjudicated**: *\"treat this as an argument you would win, not a rule you can build a business on.\"* Any **SMS fallback, OTP, or carrier-network message is squarely in scope**. **The indemnity is worthless** — it is paperwork from a judgment-proof Moroccan micro-seller, and under the FCC's 2013 *DISH Network* ruling a platform that supplies templates, schedules sends, optimizes timing, or auto-triggers messages on order events **looks like the \"maker/initiator\"** and is liable **directly**, plus **vicariously** under agency (actual authority, apparent authority, ratification). **The engineering controls are the defense.** And the **cross-subject-matter revocation prong went live 11 April 2026**: an opt-out on a **delivery notification** must now kill **marketing**. Also live: state **mini-TCPAs** (FL, OK, MD, WA CEMA, NJ), several drafted around **\"text message\"** rather than \"call\" — which **routes around *Steidinger* entirely**. And do not over-read *Steidinger v. Blackstone* (7th Cir., 14 Jul 2026): it kills the **§227(c)(5)** DNC private action for texts **only**; **§227(b)** — where the class-action money is — is untouched, and *Howard v. RNC* (9th Cir., 13 Jan 2026) went the other way. **Live circuit split.** Separately, the **highest-probability** Moroccan trigger in the whole stack sits adjacent: WhatsApp broadcast = **prospection directe** (Art 59) — *\"recipients notice it directly.\"*\n\n### 5. Shipping AI features over customer / WhatsApp content\nFour regimes fire simultaneously. **Morocco Art 12-1(b)**: sending order data and message content to Anthropic/OpenAI is *\"l'utilisation de données à caractère personnel à d'autres fins que celles pour lesquelles elles ont été collectées\"* → **AUTORISATION (F112, 2 months), not a déclaration** — *\"the single most under-appreciated trigger in the stack\"* — plus **Art 54 criminal exposure** (3 mo–1 yr + 20k–200k, doubled). **Shopify PPA**: absolute ban on using Merchant/Customer Data — *\"or enabling third parties to use\"* it — to train, fine-tune or improve any ML/AI system. **Meta Platform Terms**: solely for clients' purposes, **segregated**, no cross-client features. **GDPR Art 28(10)**: *\"if a processor infringes this Regulation by determining the purposes and means of processing, the processor shall be considered to be a controller\"* → you have breached the DPA **and you have no legal basis**. Stacked on top: **Anthropic's DPA hard-codes you as controller** when you are a processor, and **AI Act Art 50(1) disclosure binds from 2 August 2026** — **not delayed by the Digital Omnibus**, whatever the delay headlines said. And **message content will incidentally contain health, religious and political data** — *\"a COD platform processing raw message bodies cannot credibly assert it never touches sensitive data\"* (Art 12-1(a)), on which **there is no Moroccan doctrine at all** (UNCERTAIN).\n\n### 6. Publishing a retention schedule or a rights portal you haven't built\n**Both CPPA orders were mechanism failures, not policy-text failures.** **Todd Snyder — $345,178**: a misconfigured privacy portal silently dropped opt-outs **for 40 days**. **Honda — $632,500**: verification demanded before an opt-out, asymmetric choices, agent friction. **Nomi**: promised an in-store opt-out that never existed — the FTC did not allege Nomi lied about *what* it collected; **it lied about a control it offered.** *\"A 'Do Not Sell' link that doesn't work is worse than no link.\"* The same logic destroys a retention table that your **backups, your R2 media store, your blind-HMAC keyword index, and your AI vendors' logs** quietly contradict — that is simultaneously a **§5 deception** and an **Art 5(2) accountability failure**, and WP260 sets the bar at *\"phrased in a way that allows the data subject to assess, on the basis of his or her own situation, what the retention period will be.\"* **Your `/privacy#retention` table is the single sentence on this website most likely to be false on the day it ships.** Ship the deletion jobs first, then the table.\n\n### 7. Any US-hosting implication, on a site whose servers are in Germany\n**The entire marketing positioning is \"a US company.\"** That makes the US-hosting implication **the highest-probability §5 trap for this specific company** — a reader's default inference, not a claim you have to make. And it is false: VPSs are in **Germany (Contabo)**; the messaging vendor is **EU-hosted**. The precedent is exact and expensive: **GoodRx $1.5M**, **BetterHelp $7.8M**, **Avast $16.5M** (banned from selling browsing data; **$15.3M paid to 103,152 consumers in Dec 2025**) — all policies that **misdescribed data flows and third parties**. Adjacent and equally cheap to prove: calling **30 N Gould St Ste R** — *\"one of the most heavily-used mass registered-agent addresses in the US\"* — \"our headquarters\", or claiming a \"US-based team/support\" that does not exist. **A competitor or a journalist proves that in one search.** And understand the real penalty: **§5 alone carries no first-violation fine** (and after *AMG Capital* (2021) the FTC cannot get equitable monetary relief under §13(b)) — the punishment is an **injunction, a 20-year consent order, deletion and algorithmic disgorgement, and reputational kill.** The 20-year order is the sentence. Fix: **state the German hosting plainly.** *\"The mismatch is only damaging when it looks concealed.\"*\n\n### 8. A WhatsApp logo, a UI clone, or an \"Official Partner\" badge — on the page the Meta reviewer opens while deciding\n**Business Verification is a hard gate before App Review**, and the **website is itself a submitted verification field**. So the reviewer reads your marketing site while deciding whether to trust you. On it, pre-approval, they find: a partner badge you never earned, the WhatsApp glyph you have no licence to display (*\"the guidelines don't grant third parties a general marketing licence to display the logo\"* — the nominative carve-out **explicitly withholds it**), and a pixel-faithful WhatsApp-chrome clone in `#25D366`. That is **the exact \"conveys a relationship that doesn't exist\" pattern**, on the exact page, at the exact moment. Compounding it: **\"built on the WhatsApp Business Platform\" / \"official Cloud API\"** is **false today** because messaging runs through a third-party provider — *\"a reviewer who sees an unapproved applicant already claiming official-API status reads it as either misrepresentation or evidence of unofficial-access use — the latter being an independent basis for denial.\"* And **it costs you nothing commercially to avoid**: build the demo in your own design language — which is what you're actually selling — and say \"Works with WhatsApp\" in text. *\"This is the claim most likely to appear on a founder-written landing page — kill it now.\"* Separately, the same third-party stack is arguably an **Anthropic AUP breach today** (*\"circumvent the guardrails or terms of other platforms\"*) regardless of what the website says.\n\n### 9. Subscription billing without the ROSCA stack\n**Click-to-cancel (16 CFR Part 425) was VACATED IN ITS ENTIRETY by the Eighth Circuit on 8 July 2025 — six days before its compliance date. It never took effect.** Do not read that as safety. The grounds were **procedural** (the FTC skipped the preliminary regulatory analysis after its own ALJ found >$100M impact); **the substantive policy was not repudiated**, and an **ANPRM went to OIRA on 30 January 2026**. Meanwhile **ROSCA (15 U.S.C. §8403) is fully in force** and is the live vehicle: **Amazon — $2.5B** (25 Sep 2025; $1B civil penalty + $1.5B redress to ~35M consumers; **two named executives, an SVP and a VP, personally charged**); **Chegg — $7.5M**; **FTC v. Uber** pending. **All three post-date or bracket the vacatur.** A ROSCA violation is treated as an **FTC rule violation → $53,088 per violation + redress + injunction.** Then **California's ARL** (AB 2863, contracts entered/amended/extended on or after 1 July 2025) adds a remedy that should stop the room: **non-compliant goods are deemed an unconditional gift — full refund of everything ever charged.** And note what Amazon means for the founder-anonymity constraint: **personal liability survives website anonymity.**\n\n### 10. \"Worldwide\" + OFAC — and a sanctions clause copied from a template\niGrowFast LLC is a **US person**. OFAC prohibitions attach **wherever located**, and **liability is STRICT** — *\"'We didn't know the user was in Iran' is not a defense.\"* **IEEPA: greater of ~$377,700 per violation or twice the transaction value; criminal up to $1,000,000 and 20 years.** Morocco is clean; **the \"worldwide\" pitch is what creates the surface** — and it is an adjective, not a strategy. Then the template betrays you: **every ToS on the internet still lists Syria, and that is now affirmatively wrong.** **E.O. 14312** (30 Jun 2025, effective 1 Jul 2025) terminated the national emergency and revoked E.O.s 13338/13399/13460/13572/13573/13582; the **Syrian Sanctions Regulations, 31 CFR Part 542, were REMOVED from the CFR on 26 August 2025.** Publishing a stale embargo list is a false term in your own contract. Equally wrong in the other direction: describing **Russia, Belarus or Venezuela as embargoed** — they are **targeted/sectoral, not territorial**. Correct list: **Cuba, Iran, North Korea + Crimea/DNR/LNR (+Kherson, Zaporizhzhia)**. **Reference the SDN List, not a hand-maintained country list that goes stale.** And the clause is worthless without **T1.9**: screening at signup, periodic re-screening, the **50 Percent Rule**, and a **log** — *\"the record is what mitigates the penalty.\"*\n\n**Honourable mentions that did not make the ten but will still hurt:** Morocco **Art 59 prospection directe** (highest *complaint* probability of anything here); **ADA/Unruh** ($4,000/violation + fees, plaintiff-chosen forum — Wyoming's 10th Circuit does not protect you); the **accessiBe overlay trap** ($1M — never repeat a vendor's compliance claim); **Meta's missing UK DPF extension**; **Shopify PPA §9.14** vs. the core loop; **Woo §1.2.9** vs. commission pricing; **CIN capture** silently escalating every filing.\n\n---\n\n# 5. It mechanically removes iGrowFast from the OAuth verification and CASA surface entirely. Guard it. The website requirements below are cheap; the thing that costs five figures a year is a \"Connect your Google account\" button, and they do not have one. Do not add one.\n\n=====================================================================\n1. GOOGLE API SERVICES USER DATA POLICY\nSource: https://developers.google.com/terms/api-services-user-data-policy\nWorkspace overlay: https://developers.google.com/workspace/workspace-api-user-data-developer-policy\n\nDISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS (verbatim):\n- \"publish a privacy policy that fully documents how your application interacts with user data\" and list that URL in the OAuth configuration.\n- \"Your Privacy Policy and all in-product privacy notifications should be accurate, comprehensive, and easily accessible.\"\n- Disclosures must be \"prominent and timely.\"\n- Must \"accurately represent\" three things: who requests the data, what data is requested, why it is requested.\n- If data uses expand beyond original disclosures: \"update your privacy policy and prompt the user to consent to any changes.\"\n- Minimum scope: \"Don't request access to information that you don't need. Only request access to the permissions necessary to implement your application's features.\"\n\nLIMITED USE — the four obligations (verbatim):\n(a) \"Limit your use of data to providing or improving user-facing features that are prominent in the requesting application's user interface.\"\n(b) \"Transfers of data are not allowed, except: To provide or improve your appropriate access or user-facing features that are visible and prominent in the requesting application's user interface and only with the user's consent; For security purposes (for example, investigating abuse); To comply with applicable laws; or, As part of a merger, acquisition, or sale of assets of the developer after obtaining explicit prior consent from the user.\"\n(c) \"Don't allow humans to read the data, unless: You first obtained the user's affirmative agreement to view specific messages, files, or other data...; It is necessary for security purposes...; It is necessary to comply with applicable law; or The data (including derivations) is aggregated and used for internal operations in accordance with applicable privacy and other jurisdictional legal requirements.\"\n(d) Prohibited: \"Transferring or selling user data to third parties like advertising platforms, data brokers, or any information resellers\"; \"Transferring, selling, or using user data for serving ads, including retargeting, personalized or interest-based advertising\"; \"Transferring, selling, or using user data to determine credit-worthiness or for lending purposes.\"\n\n*** THE AI/ML QUESTION — DEFINITIVE ANSWER ***\nThe AI/ML clause is REAL and is in the Workspace API User Data and Developer Policy, verbatim:\n\n  \"Transferring, selling, or using user data to create, train, or improve a machine learning or artificial intelligence model beyond that specific user's personalized model for the appropriate use case or user-facing feature.\"\n\n(Note: two independent summarization passes of the base policy page reported \"no AI/ML language exists.\" That is WRONG — the clause lives in the Workspace overlay policy, which is the one that governs Sheets. Anyone researching this who only reads the base policy will reach the wrong conclusion.)\n\nDoes Limited Use prohibit sending Google-user-data to OpenAI/Anthropic? NO — NOT CATEGORICALLY. It draws a hard line between TRAINING and INFERENCE:\n\n- TRAINING on Google user data → PROHIBITED outright, except a model personalized to that specific user for that specific feature. A cross-tenant model trained on many sellers' Sheets data = violation. No consent cures this; it is not one of the enumerated exceptions.\n- INFERENCE (sending data to an LLM to produce output for the user) → this is a \"transfer to a third party\" and is PERMITTED ONLY inside exception (b): the feature must be \"visible and prominent in the requesting application's user interface\" AND have \"the user's consent.\" A background/invisible AI enrichment pass over Sheets data fails the \"prominent in the UI\" test.\n\nTherefore three conditions must ALL hold to send Sheets-sourced data to OpenAI/Anthropic:\n  1. Zero-retention / no-training API tier, contractually confirmed (both OpenAI and Anthropic API defaults do not train on API data; the retention window and abuse-monitoring human review are the exposure).\n  2. The AI feature is prominent and visible in the app UI, not a silent backend process.\n  3. Seller consent is obtained and the privacy policy discloses the AI subprocessor by name.\nCondition (c) \"don't allow humans to read the data\" is the sleeper risk: AI-provider trust-and-safety staff reviewing flagged prompts would breach this. Zero-data-retention endpoints are the mitigation.\n\n*** CRITICAL SCOPING INSIGHT — the escape hatch ***\nLimited Use governs ONLY data obtained THROUGH Google APIs. COD order data that a seller types directly into iGrowFast, or imports by CSV, is NOT Google user data and Limited Use does not touch it at all. Only the Sheets-sync path is constrained. Architecturally: keep AI features on the native data path, and they are entirely outside this policy. If AI must touch Sheets-sourced rows, the three conditions above bind. This distinction is worth designing around — it is the difference between a governed and an ungoverned AI roadmap.\n\nCompliance with this policy is INDEPENDENT of verification status: per https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13464323, all apps must comply with the API Services User Data Policy regardless of whether they are exempt from verification. The Service Account exemption removes the verification process, NOT the Limited Use obligations.\n\n=====================================================================\n2. OAUTH APP VERIFICATION\nSources: https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13463073 ; https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13464321 ; https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/brand-verification\n\nTRIGGER (verbatim): \"Apps that request access to scopes categorized as sensitive or restricted must complete Google's OAuth app verification before being granted access.\" Non-sensitive-only apps are not required to verify (but still need brand verification to show a name/logo on the consent screen). Tier is auto-labelled in the Cloud Console scope picker when you add a scope — the Console is the authoritative tier oracle.\n\nHOMEPAGE (verbatim):\n- \"The homepage must be hosted on a verified domain you own\"\n- \"The homepage must accurately represent and identify your app or brand\"\n- \"The homepage must describe your app's functionality to its users. The consent screen must also show the same exact scopes you are requesting\"\n- \"Must demonstrate the app functionalities that utilize the requested OAuth scopes\"\nPractical note for iGrowFast: the video must show the OAuth consent screen with matching branding. It does NOT require a founder on camera or any named person — a screen recording satisfies it. The founder-anonymity constraint is compatible with verification.\n\n=====================================================================\n3. That is a distinct process from OAuth verification and applies regardless.\n\n=====================================================================\n4. CASA (Cloud Application Security Assessment)\nSources: https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13465431 ; https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/restricted-scope-verification ; https://appdefensealliance.dev/casa\n\nWHEN REQUIRED (verbatim): \"Every app that requests access to Google users' restricted data and has the ability to access data from or through a third-party server must go through a security assessment.\"\nTIER THAT TRIGGERS IT: RESTRICTED SCOPES ONLY. Sensitive scopes do NOT trigger CASA — they trigger verification (video, homepage, privacy policy) but no security assessment. This is the single most important cost boundary in this whole document.\n\nFRAMEWORK: \"To standardize our security assessment we use the App Defense Alliance and the cloud application security assessment framework (CASA).\" \"CASA utilizes a risk-based, multi-tiered approach\"; apps are assigned \"either the AL1 or AL2 assurance level.\" CASA is \"based 100% on the OWASP ASVS; no proprietary requirements.\" Tier assignment is driven by data sensitivity, number of users per data type, risk tolerance, and risk indicators. \"All requirements must be satisfied for every level, the only difference between each level is the assessment method that applies.\"\n\nWHO PERFORMS IT: independent CASA-authorized labs/assessors accredited by the App Defense Alliance. Google does not perform it.\n\nCOST: Google's own statement (verbatim, https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13463817): \"Google does not charge the developer any fees for security assessment\" and \"The cost for such a service is agreed on between the developer and the assessor without any involvement from Google.\"\nUNCERTAIN — DOLLAR FIGURES: A search-engine synthesis surfaced \"$500 to $4,500 USD\" with \"2-3 weeks for tier-2, 4-6 weeks for tier-3,\" attributed to Google Workspace Marketplace docs. I fetched both Marketplace pages directly (developers.google.com/gsuite/marketplace/security-assessment and /workspace/marketplace/about-app-review) and NEITHER contains those figures — they only say \"If your app uses restricted scopes, it must also go through a security assessment.\" I therefore do NOT assert that range. The older widely-circulated \"$15,000–$75,000\" figure likewise does not appear in current official documentation. TREAT ALL PUBLISHED DOLLAR FIGURES AS UNVERIFIED; the only official position is that price is negotiated bilaterally with the assessor. Get direct quotes from multiple authorized labs.\n\nFREQUENCY (verbatim): \"All applications must be revalidated every year.\" And: \"apps must be reverified for compliance and complete a security assessment at least every 12 months after your assessor's Letter of Assessment (LOA) approval date.\" \"The required assurance level is dynamic and may increase based on changes in your user base or data-handling practices\" — i.e. growth alone can escalate the tier.\nNo free/self-service assessment tier is documented; both AL1 and AL2 are described as lab-tested/lab-verified.\n\nHOW TO AVOID CASA — three independent routes, any one suffices:\n  (i) Never request a restricted scope. Use drive.file (non-sensitive) or spreadsheets (sensitive). CASA is restricted-only.\n  (ii) Use a Service Account and no user OAuth (see §5) — removes the verification surface entirely.\n  (iii) Stay internal-only / under the exemptions in §5.\nFor iGrowFast, (i) and (ii) both already hold. They are not near CASA and should never go near it.\n\n=====================================================================\n5. *** THE CRITICAL ARCHITECTURE QUESTION — SERVICE ACCOUNT ***\nSource: https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13464323 ; https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/restricted-scope-verification ; https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13463817\n\nTHE EXEMPTION, VERBATIM (Google lists five cases where verification is NOT needed):\n  1. \"If the app is for your personal use (fewer than 100 users)\"\n  2. \"Apps in development/testing/staging mode are not subject to verification.\"\n  3. \"The app only accesses its own data (using a Service Account), and not user data (linked to a Google Account).\"\n  4. \"The app is only used by people in your Google Workspace or Cloud Identity organization\" (internal user type)\n  5. Workspace admin-trusted / Marketplace apps: \"An administrator can add a third-party app to the list of trusted apps in the Google Admin console.\"\n\nAnd verbatim from the restricted-scope verification page: \"If your app uses a service account to access only its own data, and it doesn't access any user data (linked to a Google Account), then you don't need to submit for verification.\"\n\nANSWER: YES — the Service Account model avoids OAuth verification and CASA. But the reasoning that makes it robust is MECHANICAL, not merely textual, and the textual exemption is a weaker support than it first appears. Both halves matter:\n\nTHE MECHANICAL ARGUMENT (strong, and the one to rely on):\nOAuth verification is a property of the OAuth CLIENT and its CONSENT SCREEN. A service account authenticates as ITSELF via a signed JWT assertion exchanged for a token bearing the SA's own identity. There is no consent screen, no user OAuth grant, no per-user token. Consequently:\n  - The \"unverified app\" warning screen cannot render — there is no consent screen to prepend it to.\n  - The 100-new-user cap cannot be consumed — that counter increments on user OAuth grants, of which there are zero.\n  - There is no verification submission to make — Google's verification intake is bound to an OAuth consent screen / brand configuration. A product with no consent screen has nothing to submit.\nCASA follows verification. No verification surface → no CASA. This holds regardless of which scopes the SA requests: an SA using the Sensitive `spreadsheets` scope still shows no consent screen, so scope tier is moot in the SA path. Tier only starts mattering the moment a consent screen exists.\n\nTHE TEXTUAL TENSION (be honest about this — it is the residual risk):\nThe exemption says \"accesses its own data ... and NOT user data (linked to a Google Account).\" When a Moroccan seller shares a spreadsheet they OWN with the SA's email, that spreadsheet IS data linked to a Google Account. A literal reading of the exemption is therefore ADVERSE — the SA is a Drive ACL grantee, not the owner. Google's drafting plainly contemplates the canonical case (SA owns/created the resource, e.g. its own BigQuery data), not the shared-file case.\nWeighing it: the mechanical argument dominates in practice — Google has no enforcement mechanism against a consent-screen-less SA, and Google's own FAQ blesses an adjacent shared-resource pattern verbatim: \"You can access data from your users' Google Cloud projects by creating a service account to represent your service, and then having your customers grant that service account appropriate access to their cloud data using IAM policies.\" That is precisely the share-with-the-SA topology, described approvingly. This is the strongest available authority for the pattern.\nVerdict: the SA + user-shared-sheet model does not require verification and does not incur CASA. Confidence: high on the mechanics, moderate on the letter of the exemption. This is not a five-figure annual assessment — it is nothing.\n\nLIMITS OF THE APPROACH — what breaks it:\n  a) DOMAIN-WIDE DELEGATION IS THE TRAP. If the SA is ever given DWD to impersonate users, it IS accessing user data on their behalf and verification applies for sensitive/restricted scopes. DWD is also unusable for iGrowFast's actual users: DWD requires a Google Workspace/Cloud Identity org admin. Sellers on consumer @gmail.com cannot grant it. The manual-share model is not merely acceptable — it is the ONLY option for consumer-Gmail sellers. Fortunate accident: the architecture is forced into the exempt shape.\n  b) ADDING A \"CONNECT YOUR GOOGLE ACCOUNT\" BUTTON destroys the exemption instantly. Per-user OAuth to `spreadsheets` (Sensitive) → full verification: homepage, same-domain privacy policy, demo video, Google review. Still no CASA (Sensitive ≠ Restricted) — unless someone reaches for `drive`/`drive.readonly`, which is Restricted and lands them in annual CASA. Treat a Google-account-connect button as a change requiring explicit sign-off.\n  c) LIMITED USE STILL BINDS. The exemption removes the PROCESS, not the POLICY. §1's AI/ML and transfer rules apply to Sheets-sourced data whether or not verification was ever required.\n  d) UX/OPERATIONAL COST: sellers must manually share each sheet with an unfriendly SA address (…iam.gserviceaccount.com). Support burden, not a compliance one.\n  e) SCOPE MECHANICS: `drive.file` covers only files the app created or the user opened via Picker — it does NOT cover a file manually shared with the SA. For the SA + shared-sheet flow the SA needs `spreadsheets`. Fine (no consent screen), but note this forecloses the \"just use drive.file\" answer IF they ever migrate to per-user OAuth. On that migration path they'd need `spreadsheets` (Sensitive, verification, no CASA) or a Picker-based drive.file flow (Non-sensitive, no verification) — the Picker route is the one to design toward if they ever leave the SA model.\n  f) KEY MANAGEMENT: the SA private key in Postgres Vault is now a crown-jewel credential granting access to every seller sheet ever shared with it. Compromise = cross-tenant breach of end-customer COD data with no per-user revocation granularity (sellers can individually unshare, but there is no token-revocation story). This is the real risk the SA model creates in exchange for the compliance relief. It is a GDPR/security exposure, not a Google-policy one — and given German-hosted infra processing EU-adjacent and Moroccan end-customer PII, it deserves separate attention.\n\n=====================================================================\n6. DOMAIN VERIFICATION\nSource: https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2/production-readiness/brand-verification ; https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13464321\n\n- \"You must verify that you own all domains listed in your Authorized domains section.\"\n- Method: \"Verify the ownership of your authorized domains using Google Search Console.\" An account listed as project owner or editor on the GCP project must perform the verification; a Google Account with owner permissions must be associated with the API Console project.\n- Authorized Domains must list the top-level domains of every URI: homepage, privacy policy, ToS, redirect URIs, JavaScript origins.\n\nAPEX vs SUBDOMAIN — DIRECT ANSWER: verifying the apex is sufficient and subdomains need no separate verification. Google requires verification of \"the top private domain\" (the domain available for registration on a public suffix). Google's own example, verbatim: \"an OAuth consent screen that's configured with an application home page of https://sub.example.com/product asks the account holder to verify ownership of the example.com domain.\"\nFor iGrowFast: verify igrowfast.com in Search Console once. That single verification covers app.igrowfast.com and api.igrowfast.com. Homepage on the apex + app on the subdomain is exactly the topology Google's example describes. No conflict.\nFounder-anonymity note: Search Console verification is a private control-proof (DNS TXT record or file upload) between the domain owner and Google. It publishes nothing and requires no public name. DNS TXT is the cleanest method. Compatible with the no-founder-names constraint.\n\n=====================================================================\n7. CONSEQUENCES OF AN UNVERIFIED APP\nSource: https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/7454865 ; https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/13463817\n\n- UNVERIFIED APP SCREEN: shown before the consent screen when the app uses sensitive/restricted scopes and has not completed verification.\n- 100-USER CAP (verbatim): \"New user cap\" of \"100 new users in total, after the app presents the unverified app screen.\" And: \"the user cap applies over the entire lifetime of the project, and it cannot be reset or changed.\" This is lifetime and permanent — not a rolling or resettable quota. Burning it on testing is unrecoverable without a new GCP project.\n- HARD FAILURE (verbatim): \"Failure to get your app verified before making requests to sensitive or restricted scopes will result in your project's 100 new-user cap eventually getting exhausted and Google sign-in being disabled for your users.\"\n- ADDITIONAL SIGNALS: Google Security Checkup flags the app as \"risky and unverified\"; users get notices about potential loss of functionality.\n- GRACE PERIOD: exists only in one narrow case — when Google RECLASSIFIES a scope as sensitive/restricted, existing apps get \"a grace period to go through verification before the unverified app screen and user cap are applied.\" There is no general grace period for new apps.\n- RESTRICTED SCOPES: not described as an instant hard block; they route through the same warning + cap mechanism, plus the mandatory security assessment before verification can complete.\n- Testing/dev is explicitly fine unverified: you can \"continue to build and test your app while waiting to complete verification.\"\n\nALL OF §7 IS INAPPLICABLE TO THE SA PATH — these consequences attach to the OAuth consent screen, which the SA architecture does not have. §7 is the description of what iGrowFast is avoiding, and the reason to keep avoiding it.\n\n=====================================================================\nNET ASSESSMENT FOR iGrowFast\n- Today, on the Service Account model: NO OAuth verification, NO CASA, NO 100-user cap, NO demo video. Zero Google review exposure.\n- The website requirements (homepage, same-domain privacy policy, Search Console verification) are NOT currently mandatory for Google, because nothing triggers verification. Build them anyway — they are cheap, they are required by GDPR/Moroccan reality independent of Google, and they are the prerequisite that must already exist on the day anyone proposes a Google-account-connect button. Retrofitting them under deadline is where projects fail.\n- The live, binding Google obligation today is LIMITED USE on Sheets-sourced data — specifically the prohibition on training AI/ML models on it. This constrains the AI roadmap NOW, with no verification trigger and no warning shot.\n- Highest-leverage decisions: (1) never request drive/drive.readonly; (2) never add per-user OAuth without deliberate sign-off; (3) never enable domain-wide delegation; (4) keep AI features on the native (non-Sheets) data path where Limited Use does not reach; (5) treat the SA key as the cross-tenant crown jewel it now is.\n- Two open items: exact Console tier labels for analytics/adwords scopes (confirm in the Cloud Console scope picker — it auto-labels), and real CASA pricing (only if they ever go restricted, which they should not).",

### Findings

1. **Critical — unauthorized business-owner assignment remains possible.**  
   [FILE2 §2](/Users/ismailelqorchi/Desktop/iGrowFast/New%20Website/iGrowFast/supabase/migrations/20260729150000_business_owner_parity.sql:188) lets any `super admin`, `admin`, or `business owner` satisfy `"Admins can insert users"` without constraining the inserted role. [The protection trigger](/Users/ismailelqorchi/Desktop/iGrowFast/New%20Website/iGrowFast/supabase/migrations/20260729150000_business_owner_parity.sql:2876) only examines `OLD.role` and does not fire on `INSERT` or promotion into `business owner`. With the stated table privileges, a peer admin can delete/reinsert an ordinary profile as `business owner`, particularly between FILE2 and backfill or for a business without an owner. Edge-function guards do not cover direct PostgREST table writes.  
   **Fix:** add a `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE` guard that permits transitions into `business owner` only when `auth.uid() IS NULL` or the acting database user row has role `owner`.

2. **High — a business owner can have no business.**  
   [FILE2 §4](/Users/ismailelqorchi/Desktop/iGrowFast/New%20Website/iGrowFast/supabase/migrations/20260729150000_business_owner_parity.sql:2851) permits unlimited `business owner` rows where `"DigiCom Business" IS NULL`; PostgreSQL unique indexes treat nulls as distinct by default. Such a row passes the admin helper but has inconsistent tenant scope. The platform `owner` role does not collide because it is excluded by the partial-index predicate. [PostgreSQL unique-index semantics](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/indexes-unique.html).  
   **Fix:** add `CHECK (role <> 'business owner' OR "DigiCom Business" IS NOT NULL)`; `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` is weaker because it would still permit one invalid null owner.

3. **Medium — FILE2 holds broad `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` locks longer than necessary.**  
   The 44 `ALTER POLICY` statements cover 16 tables and appear before roughly 140 KB of function/index/trigger/view work. PostgreSQL implements `ALTER POLICY` with `AccessExclusiveLock`, held until transaction end. `lock_timeout = '5s'` limits acquisition waits, not the time already-acquired locks block reads and writes. A later contested lock can therefore block previously locked tables for up to five seconds before rollback. [PostgreSQL policy implementation](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/master/src/backend/commands/policy.c).  
   **Fix:** move the large function section before the policy block and keep policy/index/trigger/view DDL in the shortest possible tail transaction; preflight `users` index-build duration.

4. **Low — `UPDATE OF role` has a documented future-trigger bypass.**  
   Direct `UPDATE users SET role=...` fires correctly, and FK-cascaded deletes fire the row-level DELETE trigger. But an earlier `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger can modify `NEW.role` during an update whose target list omitted `role`; PostgreSQL explicitly says column-specific triggers do not fire for such changes. No current repo trigger was found that mutates the role this way. [PostgreSQL trigger behavior](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createtrigger.html).  
   **Fix:** use `BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE` and retain the internal `OLD.role`/`NEW.role` comparison.

5. **Low — FILE2 is not replay-idempotent.**  
   FILE1 is idempotent through `ADD VALUE IF NOT EXISTS`. FILE2 replays successfully until `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_one_business_owner_per_biz`, which fails if the index already exists; the transaction then rolls back.  
   **Fix:** use a guarded definition check, or at minimum `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` with a separate assertion that an existing same-named index has the expected definition.

6. **Low — the helper is replaced twice.**  
   `current_user_is_business_admin()` appears at [line 31](/Users/ismailelqorchi/Desktop/iGrowFast/New%20Website/iGrowFast/supabase/migrations/20260729150000_business_owner_parity.sql:31) and again at [line 233](/Users/ismailelqorchi/Desktop/iGrowFast/New%20Website/iGrowFast/supabase/migrations/20260729150000_business_owner_parity.sql:233). They are identical today, so this is harmless but creates a future overwrite trap.  
   **Fix:** remove the second definition.

### Verified clean

- **Enum transaction:** FILE1 contains only the enum addition. FILE2 references the value in a later transaction. This is correct provided they remain separate `psql` invocations and are not combined with `--single-transaction`. PostgreSQL forbids using a newly added enum value before the adding transaction commits. [PostgreSQL `ALTER TYPE`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/sql-altertype.html).
- **Casts:** policy arrays use `text`; view arrays use `user_role`; uncast literals inside enum comparisons and `check_user_role(text[])` calls resolve from context. No mismatched cast found.
- **Policy reconciliation:** actual count is **44, not 46**: 38 `public` plus six `storage.objects` policies—three `demand_media_*` and three `stamps_*`. All 44 de-splice byte-for-byte to the captured live-catalog JSON. No missing, extra, truncated, or double-spliced statement.
- **Spot checks:** command/roles/clause placement matched for `lock_select`, both courier-note policies, `ga_connections_update_own_business`, `mediabuyer_demands_select_scoped`, `mediabuyer_payment_txns_tenant_insert`, `user_invitations_admin_revoke`, both reviewed `users` policies, `demand_media_delete_scoped`, and `stamps_write_business_admins`.
- **Functions:** all 16 edited definitions de-splice byte-for-byte to the captured `pg_get_functiondef()` files. `SECURITY DEFINER`, `STABLE`, language, return signature, and `search_path` clauses are preserved. Each contains exactly one intended splice. `seller_roster_stats` correctly remains unedited because its occurrence is comment-only.
- **Existing-function ACLs:** `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` preserves ownership and permissions. [PostgreSQL `CREATE FUNCTION`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createfunction.html).
- **Demotion/delete protection:** direct role updates and row deletes are blocked for authenticated peers; platform `owner` passes; `auth.uid() IS NULL` passes as designed; `TG_RELID`, pinned `search_path`, `SECURITY DEFINER`, and EXECUTE revocation are present.
- **View:** `security_barrier=true` is explicit. `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` preserves ownership and grants; an incompatible output column name/order/type causes the entire transaction to fail rather than silently change the contract. [PostgreSQL `CREATE VIEW`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createview.html).
- **Static lexical check:** balanced strings, dollar quotes, and parentheses.

import { useMutation, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { supabase } from '@/lib/supabase';
import {
    Dialog, DialogContent, DialogDescription, DialogFooter, DialogHeader, DialogTitle,
} from '@/components/ui/dialog';
import { Button } from '@/components/ui/button';

    Select, SelectContent, SelectItem, SelectTrigger, SelectValue,
} from '@/components/ui/select';
